## A restore from a dated backup is a TIME MACHINE — it reverts every fix since the backup, and the pin-matches-live guard then BLESSES the poison

- **footprint:** `page_components_bak_20260805_lmc` · `load_lmc.py --restore` · `decompose_lmc.py` `PINNED_REF` / `assert_pin_matches_live` · any `*_bak_<date>*` table used as a rollback source
- **the trap, in the order it fired (2026-08-12/14, loanandmortgagecalculator):**
  1. `load_lmc.py --restore <page>` restores the row from a backup **named with its date** (`20260805`) — which nobody reads as a warranty expiry. The `bugs_open/224` 0% APR fix landed **08-08**, three days after the backup. So a "safe rollback" on 08-12 quietly **reverted a shipped arithmetic fix** on a live consumer-finance calculator, and a second page lost its `btn-calculate` id (an 08-09 change).
  2. The restore was then **deployed**, so the sites repo's tip carried the pre-fix bytes.
  3. The next morning's `PINNED_REF` was taken from that tip, and `assert_pin_matches_live` **passed** — correctly, because live and pin agreed. **The guard's premise is "live is truth"; a restore makes live the lie, and the guard then certifies it.** Every seed built from that pin faithfully propagated the regression.
- **why no alarm fired:** the oracle is the only check that sees behaviour, and it is run per-task, not continuously. The regression was found **two days later** by a full sweep (6 FAILs, all `standard-calc` 0% APR — 224's exact signature). Byte gates, class counts, id sets and render proofs all passed throughout, because every one of them checks *consistency with a chosen source*, and the chosen source was the poison.
- **the check, before ANY restore from a dated backup:**
  ```bash
  # what did this page legitimately gain since the backup date? EMPTY output = safe.
  git -C ~/projects/sites log --oneline --since=2026-08-05 origin/master -- \
      loanandmortgagecalculator.co.uk/<page>.html
  ```
  A non-empty answer means the restore needs a **newer source** (the sites repo at the
  last clean commit — the rows and the repo are byte-identical on this site), not the
  backup table. And after ANY restore that got deployed: re-run the oracle for that
  tool the same hour, and treat the next `PINNED_REF` you take as suspect — pin from a
  commit that PRE-DATES your restores, not from the tip they wrote.
- **source:** the 2026-08-14 repair in `loanandmortgagecalculator_couk/NOTES`; `bugs_open/224` (the reverted fix); `bugs_open/263` (the Track B/B2 arc this happened inside).
- **added:** 2026-08-14, loanandmortgagecalculator lane

> **CORRECTION 2026-08-14 (later), to my own bullet above — `arm IS NULL` DOES find rows, and it is
> not a gap.** The bullet said *"an empty arm is never written … so `arm IS NULL` finds nothing"*. True
> only of rows written since the field shipped. The **first instrumented sweep proved otherwise within
> hours**: the 21 open items all carry an arm (stamped `2026-08-14T08:45:05Z`), while the **9 `complete`
> items carry NO `arm` key at all** — their revalidation blocks are frozen at closure (8 stamped
> `2026-08-10`, 1 `2026-08-12`), because a terminal item is never re-swept and so is never rewritten.
> So **`arm IS NULL` means "decided before 2026-08-14" — a VINTAGE marker, not an uninstrumented
> revalidator.** A "which revalidators lack arms?" query written the obvious way returns those 9 and
> reads as 9 uninstrumented items. The gap check is still `arm LIKE 'unreported:%'`. Useful corollary:
> the absence of the key now *proves* what was previously only inferred from dates — all 9 existing
> closures predate the instrument, so arm coverage of this type's history is permanently zero.

## A chassis pod's log history is ~90 SECONDS, so `logs --tail=N` answers "was this line ever emitted?" with a confident NO — and the tell is that a line you KNOW is always emitted is missing too

- **footprint:** `kubectl logs --tail`, `kubectl -n ai-persona-system logs`, `agent-chassis`, `logs -l app=`, `Strategy 6: explicit config value beat`, `Strategy 0: Resolved config path`, `build provenance`, `platform/orchestration/datahelpers/action_inputs.go`
- **fires when:** you verify a code change by grepping a pod's logs for a line the change emits — the standard post-roll question, "did my new branch actually execute?" — on any chassis pod that has been up more than a few minutes.
- **why the wrong result looks exactly right:** `--tail=200000` returns without error, the grep returns 0, and 0 reads as *"the branch never ran"* or, worse, as *"no warnings, so nothing is wrong"*. `[MEASURED 2026-08-14]` a pod started `08:58:03Z` and queried at ~13:52Z retained **243 lines spanning 92 SECONDS** (`13:51:23Z → 13:52:55Z`). 241 of the 243 were `level:info`, so **the level is not the filter and raising verbosity will not help.** The window is not the pod's lifetime; it is roughly the last minute and a half, whatever `--tail` you pass. An absence here is bounded by retention, and retention is far shorter than anyone's intuition.
- **the check:** put a line you KNOW fires constantly into the SAME filter as the line you are hunting, and make it a liveness control. If the control is also absent, you have measured retention and learnt nothing:
  ```bash
  # WRONG — a confident zero that means nothing
  kubectl -n ai-persona-system logs <pod> --tail=200000 | grep -c 'my new log line'

  # RIGHT — stream every replica, control line in the same alternation
  for p in $(kubectl -n ai-persona-system get pods -l app=agent-chassis -o name); do
    kubectl -n ai-persona-system logs -f "${p#pod/}" --since=1s 2>/dev/null \
      | grep --line-buffered -E "my new log line|Strategy 0: Resolved config path" &
  done
  ```
  `Strategy 0: Resolved config path` is a good general control for anything in the input resolver — it fires on most steps. Then WAIT: the two lines this recipe was written for took **~14 minutes** of real traffic to appear.
- **the adjacent trap — this is the same fact that retires the `build provenance` recipe, and for a different reason.** The provenance stamp is a STARTUP line, so it is out of range within minutes for a *different* cause (it is emitted once, at the front). Its fallback is the binary probe (`grep -aq "<sha>" /proc/1/exe` with a two-sided control). **There is no binary-probe equivalent for a runtime branch**, which is why streaming is the only answer for "did it execute?" — and why an offline detector or a `doc_notes` writer beats a log line for anything you will need to prove later.
- **also worth knowing:** a log-only signal is therefore NOT a durable control on this fleet, and a council seat will say so — `bug_historian` objected on exactly this ground to a change whose rejection arms logged and did nothing else, and the objection was then confirmed by the author hitting this trap while verifying that same change. If a mechanism's refusal needs to be *auditable*, it must write a row, not a line.
- **REFINED 2026-08-19 (webdesign_tool_rebuilds lane) — re-measured at 2.2 MINUTES, and `--since` is not a way round it: the FIRST question is whether the branch's effect is a ROW, because then you should not be reading logs at all.** `[MEASURED 2026-08-19 21:04Z]` both `v1.0.1316` replicas, asked for **six hours** (`logs --since=6h`), returned 458 and 1,110 lines beginning at `21:01:50Z` / `21:02:07Z` — a window of ~2m10s, i.e. `--since` is silently clamped by rotation and reads as if the service was quiet before then. The trap fired verifying RFC_036 §9.3: the new fork branch logs `library tool claims this function`, the build ran at `20:57`, and the grep at `21:03` returned 0 on both pods. **The reason that 0 never became a finding is the control in this entry** — `CreateToolComponentAction`'s own unconditional "Creating tool" line was absent too, and the earliest retained timestamp then measured the window. **What is new: the branch also WRITES `content_components.forked_from`, and that column is only reachable from the branch, so the row proved execution in one query with no timing constraint at all.** Generalise it: before reaching for a log line, ask what the branch CHANGED — a column, an item, a doc_note — and assert that instead. A log line proves the code *spoke*; the row proves it *acted*, and it is still there tomorrow. Streaming (above) remains the answer only when the branch's sole effect really is the line.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/231` (the change this was measured on; CTS-059) · MEMORY `prove-a-deploy-at-the-artefact-index` and `logs-deploy-reads-one-pod-of-n` · MEMORY `log-measurement-discipline` (absence bounded by retention, pod age AND rotation) · MEMORY `a-silent-gate-either-did-not-look-or-approved` (the same two-causes-one-reading shape) · `016b` §9 "no error anywhere usually means no error surface"
- **source:** 2026-08-14, bugfix_209/231 lane, post-roll verification of Strategy 6 on chassis `v1.0.1298`. First read: 0 matches across both replicas, which I nearly recorded as "not yet exercised". The control (Strategy 0's pre-existing line, also absent) is the only reason that did not happen; streaming then produced 6 matches across both pods in ~35 minutes.
- **added:** 2026-08-14, bugfix_209/231 lane

### ~~The fleet's LLM capability is DOWN until 2026-09-01~~ — RESOLVED 2026-08-14 ~17:05Z (cap raised). KEPT because the 400 reads like a bad request and the attribution trap is the reusable part

- **footprint:** `llm_call_log` (`success`, `error_message`), `platform/aiservice/*`, any `execute_ai_step` action, `orchestration_states.error` containing `AI unavailable`, every diagnosis / council / audit / content agent, `diagnosis_artifacts` (bundles land, verdicts do not)
- **fires when:** anything in the fleet calls an LLM, from 2026-08-14 ~15:36Z onward. **No symptom of a quota anywhere obvious:** the failure arrives as `API request failed with status 400: invalid_request_error`, which reads as a malformed request — so the instinct is to doubt your prompt, your payload, your image encoding or your step config. All of those are fine. Read the message body: *"You have reached your specified API usage limits. You will regain access on **2026-09-01 at 00:00 UTC**."*
- **why the wrong answer looks right:** a 400 is the status code for *your* mistake, and it sits beside genuinely malformed sibling errors in the same table (3 rows the same afternoon were a real `messages.0.content.1.image.source.base64.data` fault). A run also gets **most** of the way through before dying — a `090` diagnosis on 08-14 built a **54,805-char evidence bundle** and then failed only at its `verdict` step, so `diagnosis_artifacts` has a row and the work item reads `triaged` with `error` beginning `AI unavailable`. That looks like a flaky step worth retrying. **It is not; it will fail identically until the cap resets or is raised**, and each retry burns a dispatch.
- **the check — one query, and read `success`, not the token columns:**
  ```sql
  SELECT date_trunc('hour',created_at)::time AS hr, count(*) AS calls,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE success) AS ok, count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT success) AS failed
  FROM llm_call_log WHERE created_at > now()-interval '6 hours' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;
  SELECT left(error_message,200), count(*) FROM llm_call_log
   WHERE NOT success AND created_at > now()-interval '6 hours' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
  ```
  ⚠ **Do not diagnose this from `input_tokens`.** A failed call logs NULL/0 tokens, so a token-based census shows the hour getting *cheaper* exactly as it stops working — 08-14 read `17 calls, 0 input tokens` for the 16:00 hour, which looks like idle rather than dead.
- **⚠ THE ATTRIBUTION TRAP, and it nearly produced a badly wrong report.** The cap was hit hours after a lane deliberately enabled `improvement-sweep`, whose burst was measured at **6.0x baseline** — so "my burst exhausted the account" was the obvious and alarming reading. **It is false, by two orders of magnitude.** The cap is **MONTHLY**: August had consumed **~221.9M input tokens** by 08-14, dominated by 08-09 (42.7M), 08-08 (33.2M), 08-10 (26.2M) and 08-04 (24.9M). The sweep's whole attributable contribution was **~0.71M ≈ 0.3% of the month**. Daily spend had in fact *fallen* an order of magnitude by 08-13 (1.7M). **Before blaming a recent action for a period-scoped limit, get the period's denominator** — a day's spend is not evidence about a month's cap, however dramatic the day.
- **✅ RESOLVED 2026-08-14 ~17:05Z — the cap was raised, well before the stated 09-01 reset.** Verified with a **demand control**, not by absence: `llm_call_log` had ZERO calls between 16:42 and 17:05, so "no failures" proved nothing — I re-armed a stranded diagnosis run to force real traffic, and it produced **2 successful calls, 0 failed**, then completed. ⚠ **This is the reusable half of the entry: a quota outage cannot be declared over from an absence of failures.** Something must call. If you read this entry during a future outage, the resolution date above is the LAST one, not a rule — check `success` yourself.
- **what to do while it lasts:** nothing in code fixes it. It is a **specified** (configured) account limit, so the owner can raise it; otherwise capability returns 2026-09-01 00:00 UTC. Until then: expect every LLM-dependent mechanism to fail, do **not** re-run diagnosis/council/audit work hoping for a different outcome, and treat any `0 findings` from an LLM-backed check as **unknown**, never as clean.
- **source:** 2026-08-14, `bugfix_213_verifier_producer_join` lane, found while chasing why a filed `090` verdict step failed · `llm_call_log` request_id `req_011Ce2yVrKM5fTwcXyySxMFm`
- **added:** 2026-08-14, bugfix_213 lane

### Clearing a claim from `content_data` and firing a rerender publishes the claim UNCHANGED — the assemble-only rerender never regenerates `rendered_html`

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/actions/rerender_single_page_action.go` (`RerenderSinglePageAction`), `page_components.rendered_html`, `page_components.content_data`, `page-rerender` (agent), any `page_rerender` dispatch with NO `spec.reason`, `platform/orchestration/actions/discovery_checks/check_unverified_claims.go` (`ScanDeployedClaims`), `claims_unverified` / `stat_unit_impossible` work items
- **fires when:** you correct published copy by editing `page_components.content_data` and then re-rendering the page — the obvious two-step, and the one the `claims_unverified` item's own stored `fix` text appears to prescribe: *"should be cleared in `page_components.content_data`, NOT only in the rendered HTML — a re-render would otherwise reprint it."* That sentence is true of the **content-regenerating** routes and false of the **assemble** route, and it does not say which one you are about to fire.
- **the tell: there is none.** The orchestration reaches `COMPLETED`, the deploy commits, `pages.deployed_at` moves, and the served page is byte-for-byte the old copy plus whatever else changed. `RerenderSinglePageAction`'s own file header says it outright — *"Simple concatenation - no template re-rendering"* — it assembles the page from **stored per-component `rendered_html`** and contains no `UPDATE page_components` at all. So the surface you edited is not the surface it publishes. The next audit re-reports the same finding, which reads as the check being broken or the fix not having deployed, and both of those are much more interesting-looking than the truth.
- **the check, before you dispatch:** `grep -c "UPDATE page_components" platform/orchestration/actions/<the action you are about to fire>.go`. **Zero means it does not write that table**, whatever its name implies (`rerender_single_page_action.go`: 0). Then assert on the artefact, not the status: `curl` the page and grep for the string you removed, with a fabricated-URL control on the same domain, and check the byte delta equals the length of what you deleted.
- **and the audit reads BOTH surfaces anyway, so one edit was never enough:** `ScanDeployedClaims` runs `scanComponentClaims` over **`rendered_html`** (banned claims, unregistered numbers) and `scanStoredStatClaims` over **`content_data`** (stat fields), and the revalidator's claim-granular gate searches `ExaminedTextBySlot`, which is built as `html + contentJSON`. A one-surface edit therefore leaves the finding standing whichever surface you picked. Edit both, in one transaction each, guarded.
- **do NOT reach for the section editor to regenerate it** on a `claims_unverified` item: that path is an LLM rewrite, and this item type is HITL-terminal precisely because *"Truth decisions are human — do not auto-rewrite"* (`check_unverified_claims.go`). A minimal deletion applied to both stored surfaces is the human act the item asks for; a regeneration is the act it forbids.
- **source:** 2026-08-14, bugfix_168 lane, cleaning `leopardessconsulting.co.uk/case-studies` on the owner's instruction so the three revalidation gates could be observed. The single-edit plan was written down and would have shipped a no-op that looked like a fix; caught by reading the action before firing it, not by a symptom. Both surfaces then edited (-36 chars each), and the served page moved 24,558 -> 24,522 bytes with the control still 404ing.
- **relations:** `docs024_key_docs_latest/bugfix_168_deployed_asset_path/NOTES_deployed_asset_path.md` (2026-08-14 afternoon) · MEMORY `a-complete-work-item-is-not-a-repaired-artefact` and `prove-a-deploy-at-the-artefact-index` (same shape: a terminal status is not an artefact) · the `page_id` not `page_name` trap on the same action, filed 2026-07-30 by the leopardess nav lane
- **added:** 2026-08-14, bugfix_168 lane

### An image placed INSIDE a guide's prose is destroyed by the next body rewrite, silently — imagery and prose share ONE overwritable llm-owned field

- **footprint:** `content_components` `article-body` (id `5835b2e1-50d7-4f20-8a9c-8da4d270ae3d`, **93 instances / 18 sites** measured 2026-08-14 19:30 — it was 91/17 the previous day, so re-count rather than quoting this), `page_components.content_data->>'content'`, `save_page_sections_overwrite`, `page_component_history`, any `<figure>`/`<img>` hand-placed or agent-placed into article prose
- **fires when:** you illustrate a blog/guide article by putting a `<figure><img><figcaption>` into the article body — which is the ONLY way to place an image mid-prose today, and it works, deploys and looks permanent
- **the tell: there is none, and the artefact stays healthy.** `article-body` has exactly ONE field — `content`, `type: text`, `source: "llm"` — so the picture and the words are the same overwritable blob. Any wholesale prose regeneration replaces both. The asset keeps serving 200, the work item completes, the page deploys, and no check compares "images before" with "images after". **Measured on `dartsonline.com/blog/flight-shapes.html` (`page_id 73f9e8ad-30f9-4383-9452-5164e6a3ca1a`): `page_component_history` archived the body at `2026-08-05 11:52:48.095654`, 4018 chars, containing `<img` and the illustration ref; the current row was written at `11:52:48.185471`, 6207 chars, containing neither, `source = save_page_sections_overwrite`. Ninety milliseconds, and nine days before anyone noticed.** The 08-05 session lost 3–4 of its own placements the same way *inside one session* and wrote the prediction down; it still cost the next reader (me) a wrong bug filing.
- **the check, and it is one query:** never conclude "this asset was never wired" from a present-tense scan of `rendered_html`/`content_data` — that cannot distinguish *never placed* from *placed and overwritten*. Ask the history instead:
  ```sql
  SELECT created_at, source, length(content_data->>'content') AS len,
         (content_data::text ILIKE '%<img%') AS had_img
  FROM page_component_history WHERE page_id = '<page>' ORDER BY created_at;
  ```
  A `true` that becomes a `false` is a destroyed placement, not an orphan. **Before placing a guide image at all, know it is ephemeral** — and after any content rewrite of an illustrated page, re-check the image survived rather than trusting the completed item.
- **do NOT file this against `bugs_open/114`** ("generated, deployed, and nothing points a page at it"). It is the opposite direction: the page DID point at it. It is the `save` REPLACES / `rerender` MERGES class of `bugs_open/238`, with the no-archive/no-warning shape of `226` / `229`. I filed it as 114 first and had to correct it; the correction is at the foot of that file.
- **source:** 2026-08-14, owner asked for explanatory images in the dartsonline guides; found while investigating why the flight-shapes diagram was absent. Restored verbatim from `page_component_history` under a guarded UPDATE (work item `aaabecaa-b69c-472d-8a3a-e004d1215b05`) — **a one-page stopgap the next rewrite will undo, not a fix.** Durable design in progress: `docs024_key_docs_latest/inline_guide_imagery/`
- **relations:** `dartsonline_traffic/README_where_we_are.md` 2026-08-05 (the session that placed all 8 and predicted the loss) · `bugs_open/114` (the correction) · `bugs_open/238` / `226` / `229` (the real class) · MEMORY `a-complete-work-item-is-not-a-repaired-artefact`
- **added:** 2026-08-14

### `content_direction.formatted` is section-ordered by Go MAP ITERATION — so a before/after diff of it is pure noise, and the obvious way to verify a spec edit tells you nothing

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/datahelpers/format_content_direction.go`, `FormatContentDirection`, `FormatSpecValue`, `site_specs` (`aspect='content_direction'`), `write_site_spec`, `apply_adoption_plan`
- **fires when:** you edit a site's `content_direction` and then try to verify the edit landed by diffing the old and new `formatted` strings — the natural check, and the one the existing "you MUST regenerate `formatted`" landmines above will send you to.
- **the tell: there is none, and it fails in BOTH directions.** `FormatContentDirection` does `for key, val := range spec` over a `map[string]interface{}`, and Go randomises map iteration order **per run**. So the top-level sections (`Voice:`, `Writing rules:`, `Example phrases:` …) come out in a different order every single time it is called, even for byte-identical input. Consequences, both bad:
  - **a diff of a GOOD edit looks catastrophic** — the whole block reads as changed, and a session checking "did I break something?" sees maximum damage and may revert a correct change;
  - **a diff cannot confirm a BAD edit either** — the noise floor is the entire document, so a genuinely missing replacement is invisible in it.
  Length is no help either: it moves for reordering-independent reasons and is not a content check.
- **the check — verify by CONTENT, never by diff, and assert BOTH directions:**
  ```sql
  SELECT data->>'formatted' LIKE '%<the phrase you removed>%'   AS should_be_false,
         data->>'formatted' LIKE '%<a phrase that must SURVIVE>%' AS should_be_true
  FROM site_specs WHERE site_id='<id>' AND aspect='content_direction' AND is_current;
  ```
  The survive-clause is the load-bearing half: a copy edit that "removes negativity" can silently become a deletion of the site's honest caveats, and a removed-phrase check alone reports that as success. Put both in a `DO`/`RAISE` block in the same transaction as the write — a `SELECT` verify block cannot stop a `COMMIT`.
- **and do not hand-replicate the formatter to compute the new value.** Call the real one: a scratch Go module with `replace github.com/gqls/agentchassis => /home/ant/projects/agentchassis`, importing `datahelpers` and calling `FormatContentDirection` directly, is ~30 lines and cannot drift from production. Hand-copying it is how the two halves diverge silently.
- **while you are here: Go `len()` on the result counts BYTES, Postgres `length()` and Python `len()` count CHARACTERS.** On a spec full of em-dashes these differ by hundreds (measured: 11,327 vs 11,249 on the same string). Neither is wrong; quoting them side by side reads as a truncation bug that is not there.
- **source:** 2026-08-14, brochure_component_library contrast front, rewriting `fundamentallyai.com`'s `content_direction` into positive-definition form on the owner's instruction. Found by reading the formatter before trusting a diff, not by a symptom — the diff would have been the natural next step and would have been uninterpretable. Distinct from the two existing `formatted` entries above, which say *regenerate it or your edit is invisible*; this one says *once you have regenerated it, the obvious verification is useless*.
- **relations:** the `content_direction.formatted` entries above (same field, the prior half of the trap) · MEMORY `mutate-the-code-to-prove-the-guard` and `a-post-fix-zero-needs-a-demand-control` (same shape: a check that cannot come out the other way) · `fleet_copy_quality/CONTRIB_2026-08-12_the_honest_ban_and_the_voice_gate_nobody_opted_into.md` (the fleet lane that regenerated `formatted` on 14 sites)
- **added:** 2026-08-14, brochure_component_library contrast front

## A census keyed on a CORRUPTION MARKER is not a work-list: it includes rows you must never republish, and it cannot see your predecessor's deliberate skip

- **footprint:** `assets.filename` / `assets.url` `LIKE '%asset-key%'` · `assets.status` · `site_work_items` `item_type='undeployed_asset'` · `bugs_open/248`'s drain buckets · any "re-trigger every row matching X" batch
- **the trap, and why the wrong answer looks right:** the marker query selects rows whose **bookkeeping** is wrong. That is a different set from rows whose **artefact** is wrong, and it silently contains two classes that must not be acted on:
  1. **`superseded` / `retired` rows.** Measured 2026-08-14: 98 marked rows = **87 active + 10 superseded + 1 retired**. Their bytes have been REPLACED by a newer asset, so redeploying pushes a stale image over a current one. **A wire check does NOT catch this** — the old path may legitimately 404, so the row looks like honest outstanding work. Only `AND a.status='active'` catches it.
  2. **Rows a previous session deliberately LEFT.** After `248`'s bucket-A pilot, the two rows still showing `unresolved` were exactly the two that pilot **skipped on purpose** as live-referenced 200s (leopardess `logo` — itself `retired` — and finetuning `logo`, both serving `logo.png` 200). Promoting them "because the pilot proved that action" reproduces the precise regression the pilot avoided. **Nothing in the row, the item or the census records that a human decided not to act**; the reason lives only in a bug-file contribution.
- **the check, before a row count becomes a target list:**
  ```sql
  -- 1. never republish a non-active asset
  SELECT status, count(*) FROM assets
  WHERE filename LIKE '%asset-key%' OR url LIKE '%asset-key%' GROUP BY 1;
  -- 2. bucket per ASSET (bool_or), or your buckets will not sum:
  --    the earlier per-item join reconciled to 133 of 140 because one asset can match several items
  ```
  then `curl` the reader-derived path per row, **and grep the bug file for the site** — a residual of one or two immediately after a pilot is a **skip signal** far more often than an omission.
- **the general form, which is the part worth carrying:** a batch built from `WHERE <marker>` inherits every assumption the marker encodes and none of the judgement a human applied afterwards. Bucketing by state turned "re-trigger 140 rows" into "26 need nothing, 13 one action, 64 another, 30 a check first" — and re-measuring after the pilot turned the remaining "2 to promote" into "0, and touching them is a regression".
- **source:** `bugs_open/248` (CONTRIBUTION 2026-08-14 late); `staged_component_build/HANDOFF_2026-08-14c_continue_here.md` §1; NOTES `## 2026-08-14 (c)`. Sibling entry on the same table: "`assets.url` holding a placeholder is NOT the outage…" (2026-08-10) — that one is about over-reading the count, this one about acting on it.
- **added:** 2026-08-14, staged_component_build

## `write_audit_findings` drops a JSON OBJECT silently and routes on `category`, not on the `work_item_type` your prompt carefully asks for — so a new auditor can file NOTHING, for weeks, while every step reports success

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/actions/write_audit_findings_action.go` · any `agent_definitions` step with `"action": "write_audit_findings"` · the config key `findings_field` · `site_work_items.spec->>'audit_source'` · adding or reviewing ANY site auditor
- **the trap, both halves, and each one looks exactly like success:**
  1. **The parse switch has `case string:` and `case []interface{}:` and NO `case map[string]interface{}:`** (lines ~537-587). So if your prompt asks for `{"summary": …, "findings": [...]}` — the natural shape when an audit has a headline as well as a list — and `findings_field` points at that object, `findings` stays nil and the action returns `{"items_created": 0, "reason": "no valid findings"}`. **The step SUCCEEDS. The orchestration reaches `complete`. The run has an `error` of NULL.** `bugs_open/272` (filed 2026-08-14) is the instance: `site-review-agent` has asked for an object since at least migration 340 and has filed **zero** work items in its entire history — `[MEASURED]` no row anywhere in `site_work_items` carries `spec->>'audit_source' = 'site-review'`, while the four producers that prompt for a bare array all have rows. It runs inside every improvement sweep, so this was ~16 LLM calls a fortnight producing nothing, invisibly.
  2. **`work_item_type` in a finding is read by NOTHING.** Routing is `classifyFinding`, deterministic in Go, on `category` + whether the named page exists in `pages`. `site-review-agent`'s prompt requires `work_item_type` in every finding and lists five allowed values; that field is discarded. Worse, an **off-vocabulary `category` does not fail** — it mints `item_type = "audit_finding_" + category` aimed at `content-gap-planner`, an item type no verifier knows. `[MEASURED]` 6 such rows exist fleet-wide (`audit_finding_brief_fidelity` ×5, `audit_finding_audience`), 5 still `detected`.
- **the check, before you believe a new or edited auditor works — it is one query and it must be a PAIR:**
  ```sql
  SELECT jsonb_typeof(collected_data#>'{<your_llm_step>,result}')              AS result_shape,
         jsonb_array_length(collected_data#>'{<your_llm_step>,result,findings}') AS llm_found,
         collected_data#>>'{<your_write_step>,items_created}'                    AS items_created,
         collected_data#>>'{<your_write_step>,audit_source}'                     AS stamped_source
  FROM orchestration_states WHERE orchestration_id = '<your run>';
  ```
  **`items_created = 0` on its own proves nothing** — it is also exactly what a genuinely clean site looks like, which is why this survived so long. Only the PAIR discriminates: LLM found N > 0 with `items_created = 0` is this bug. An empty `stamped_source` is the same signal from the other side: the zero-findings branch returns a result map with no `audit_source` key at all, so the field being blank means the writer never reached the point where it stamps one.
- **the fix when you are AUTHORING one (cheaper than inheriting the bug):** either prompt for a **bare JSON array** (what `brief-fidelity-auditor`, `content-quality-auditor` and `visual-design-auditor` do, and their rows exist), or return an object and point `findings_field` at the **array inside it** — `<step>.result.findings`, not `<step>.result`. `ExtractNestedField` walks arbitrary depth, so the deeper path costs nothing. Then assert the string in your migration's verify block: the failure mode is silence, and silence does not draw attention later. Worked example: `sql_for_agents/408_offer_analyser_agent.sql` (`offer-analyser`, which returns an object because it has two outputs, and whose guard refuses any other `findings_field`).
- **while you are here:** `page` must be the EXACT `pages.name` (only `homepage`/`home` → `index` is aliased). A paraphrased page name is not an error either — it falls through to "the page does not exist" and becomes `needs_content_planning`, i.e. *create a new page*, when you meant *fix this one*.
- **source:** 2026-08-14, vigilant_designer_offer_analysis lane, building B4 (`offer-analyser`) on this write path. Found by reading the action before wiring to it, and confirmed by the audit_source census above — not by a symptom, because there is no symptom to have. `bugs_open/272` holds the site-review instance and its fix candidates; `bugs_closed/264` is the sibling defect on the same config line (four auditors' findings all landing under one producer name).
- **relations:** `bugs_open/272` · `bugs_closed/264` · register **BIZ-032** (the auditor built against this trap) · MEMORY [[a-post-fix-zero-needs-a-demand-control]] (the zero that needs a demand control — this is that shape exactly) and [[writes-the-field-is-not-reads-the-field]] (`work_item_type`: written by the prompt, read by nobody)
- **added:** 2026-08-14, vigilant_designer_offer_analysis

### `deferred` is the ONLY parking state for a work item — a `blocked` one un-parks itself within 600s, and only if its handler exists, so the same park behaves oppositely on two rows that look identical

- **footprint:** `site_work_items` (`status`, `handler_agent`), `scheduled_tasks` row **`feasibility-recheck`** (`pre_query`), `platform/orchestration/actions/claim_work_item_action.go` (the handler-registration check, ~:125-160), `internal/core-manager/admin/site_admin_handlers.go` (`HandleRetryWorkItem` ~:877, `resolve` ~:930), `platform/orchestration/actions/load_work_item_actions.go:651`, any attempt to HOLD a work item so it cannot run
- **fires when:** you need a filed work item **not to run yet** — gating a change behind a human's look, staging a rollout, holding a canary. There is no symptom either way: a held item and a stuck item are the same row to the eye, and a park that silently expires looks exactly like a park that held until you find the work already done.
- **the trap, and it is two-sided:**
  - **`blocked` is NOT a park.** `feasibility-recheck` is a **live, enabled** `scheduled_tasks` row (600s) whose `pre_query` is `UPDATE site_work_items SET status='triaged', error=NULL WHERE wi.status='blocked' AND EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM agent_definitions ad WHERE ad.type = wi.handler_agent AND ad.deleted_at IS NULL)`. An item parked by blocking is **promoted back to claimable within one tick** — automatically, by a task nobody in the conversation mentioned.
  - **…unless its `handler_agent` is empty, in which case `blocked` is permanent** — the `EXISTS` fails, nothing rescues it, and the item jams for ever. **So the SAME parking action produces opposite outcomes on two rows that differ only in a column you were not looking at**, and the un-parkable one is the *malformed* row. Fixing a row's handler (correct, desirable) converts its `blocked` state from a permanent trap into a self-healing one — i.e. **repairing an item can silently remove a park you were relying on.**
- **the check, before trusting any hold:** park with **`status='deferred'`** and verify against the claim predicates, not against intuition — `claim_work_item_action.go:102` and `load_work_item_actions.go:651` both filter `status IN ('triaged','approved')`, and `deferred` is in no promoter's `WHERE`: `triage_detect_items_action.go` takes `status='detected'` only, `HandleRetryWorkItem` takes `{needs_human_review, failed, blocked, unresolved}`, the resolve endpoint takes that set plus `triaged`, the stale-item reaper takes `triaged` + `pipeline='build'`, and `feasibility-recheck` takes `blocked`. Guard the park itself so it cannot race a claim: `UPDATE … SET status='deferred' WHERE id=$1 AND status='triaged'`.
- **and enumerate the promoters by QUERY, not by memory.** Two lanes independently listed the un-park paths they could think of, published the list, and both lists were missing `feasibility-recheck` — it lives in a **`scheduled_tasks` row**, so no amount of Go grepping finds it: `SELECT name, enabled, interval_seconds, pre_query FROM scheduled_tasks WHERE pre_query ILIKE '%site_work_items%';`. One list was presented as a six-row table, which is a very convincing way to publish an unenumerated absence.
- **source:** 2026-08-14, `bugs_open/122` ink-derivation lane + the filing lane, holding a dartsonline stylesheet rebuild behind an owner's visual gate. Found by following a comment in `claim_work_item_action.go` after a peer corrected a *different* wrong theory about the same column — three successive theories about one empty `handler_agent` (it will fire early / it will fire via operator retry / it will jam), only the third correct, and none reached by whoever held the previous one.
- **relations:** the sibling entry above on work-item **first-class columns vs `spec`** — the same `handler_agent` column, from the writing side; that one is why the row was malformed here · MEMORY [[a-silent-gate-either-did-not-look-or-approved]] (a park that expires and a park that holds are the same row until you query) · [[check-the-no-op-case-not-only-the-damage-case]]
- **added:** 2026-08-14, bugfix_122 ink-derivation thread

### A timing guard that fails silently hands you a complete, well-formed measurement of the WRONG MOMENT — and a "nothing changed" reading is exactly what a run that never happened looks like

- **footprint:** `scheduled_tasks` (`last_triggered_at`, `interval_seconds`), any `sleep … ; <query>` compound shell used to wait for a scheduled run, `date -u -d '<literal>'`, `result->'revalidation'` and any other **last-write-wins** per-row stamp read after a sweep (`site_work_items`), `orchestration_states` polled for a dispatch
- **fires when:** you wait for something the cluster does on a clock — a daily sweep, a scheduled dispatch, a reaper tick — and then measure. No symptom either way: the measurement succeeds, every figure in it is correct, and only the *moment* it describes is wrong.
- **the trap, in two independent halves that compound:**
  - **`date -d` parses in LOCAL time; `-u` only formats the OUTPUT.** `date -u -d '2026-08-15 08:46:30' +%s` on a BST box yields 07:46:30Z, an hour early — and if that is already past, the arithmetic goes negative and `sleep` exits with a usage error instead of waiting.
  - **A compound command carries on after a failed step.** Without `set -e`, `sleep -839; psql …` runs the queries *immediately*. You get a full, correctly-formatted result set that describes the instant BEFORE the thing you were waiting for.
- **why it is worse than an ordinary stale read:** for a last-write-wins stamp, the pre-run and post-run readings are **structurally identical** — same arms, same columns, same counts whenever nothing moved. So *"the sweep ran and nothing changed"* and *"the sweep has not run"* render as the same table, and a prediction of "no change" reads as CONFIRMED by a measurement that could not have disconfirmed it. This is the same hazard as reading a per-row revalidation stamp as a run log, arriving from the timing side instead of the aggregation side.
- **the check:** **never read a measurement of a scheduled run without the anchor and a clock stamp in the same output.** One extra line, and it is what caught this:
  ```sql
  SELECT name, last_triggered_at FROM scheduled_tasks WHERE name = '<the task>';
  ```
  plus `date -u '+%H:%M:%SZ'` in the same command. If the anchor has not moved, nothing below it is a post-run reading, whatever it says.
- **and prefer a CONDITION to a clock.** Poll the anchor until it *changes*, then measure — immune to timezone arithmetic entirely. Make the timeout branch say what it means: *"the anchor never moved — the daily did not fire, which is a finding, not a timeout"*, so a scheduler that has genuinely stopped cannot read as a tooling failure.
- **source:** 2026-08-15, bugfix_168 lane, waiting for the `review-queue-revalidate-daily` sweep to test a pre-committed prediction. Caught within seconds because the query block already carried `last_triggered_at` — by habit, not by suspicion. Had it not, the prediction would have been recorded as confirmed against a reading taken 45 minutes before the run.
- **relations:** MEMORY [[pin-the-clock-to-before-the-failure]] and [[a-baseline-that-reads-head-expires-when-you-commit]] (both are "the measurement answers the question you encoded, at the moment you encoded it") · the `arm` last-write-wins entry filed by this lane 2026-08-12 · [[two-clean-runs-cannot-establish-stability]]
- **added:** 2026-08-15, bugfix_168 deployed_asset_path lane

### An unsupported-claim count is a COMPARISON, so the register moves it without anyone touching the page — and the half that moves it is not in `data->'facts'`

- **footprint:** `site_specs` where `aspect='evidence_base'` (**both** `data->'facts'` and `data->'banned_claims'`), `site_work_items` of `item_type='claims_unverified'` (`result->'revalidation'->>'reason'`, `evidence->'by_check'`), `platform/orchestration/actions/evidence_citations.go:222`, `platform/orchestration/datahelpers/claims_global.go`, any diff of two `site_specs` versions
- **fires when:** you read a `claims_unverified` finding count, or you compare two versions of a register to explain one. No symptom: every count is correct, the checker is working exactly as designed, and the page you are about to investigate is innocent.
- **the trap, in three layers that stack:**
  - **The count is not a property of the page.** It is `page × register`, and **either side moves it**. Measured 2026-08-15: `a355d78b` (webdesign.uk `index-rejected-v1-20260806`) went **14 → 19** overnight on a page whose `newest_component_update` is `2026-08-05` — untouched for ten days, `deployed_at` NULL, never served. The cause was an **owner re-attestation** at `2026-08-14 20:13:21Z` retiring the *"three or four days"* build time in favour of *"usually ready the next day"*, which added a **28th banned-claim pattern**. A reader who sees "still carries 19 claim(s)" and goes hunting for a page edit finds nothing and starts to doubt the checker. **This is the mechanism working: an owner changed what is true, and every page still saying the old thing was re-flagged within one sweep.**
  - **`banned_claims` is NOT a separate `aspect` — it lives INSIDE the `evidence_base` row's `data`** (`evidence_citations.go:222` seeds `{"facts": [], "banned_claims": []}`). So `WHERE aspect ILIKE '%banned%'` returns **0 rows for a site holding 28 of them**, and reads as "this site has no banned-claims list". Diffing `data->'facts'` alone therefore declares a register unchanged while its *enforcement* half has moved.
  - **A projection diff cannot see a change in a key it did not select — and `kind: capability` facts have NO `value` and NO `tolerance`.** A sensible-looking diff over `id`/`value`/`tolerance` returned **0 rows** across a boundary where a fact genuinely changed, because the change was in `claim` / `writer_line` / `source`. Two independent zero-results, both false, both entirely plausible, both pointing at the wrong cause (a binary roll 23 minutes later, which was innocent).
- **the check:** **diff whole objects first, project second** — a projection can only find changes in the keys you already suspected. Order-insensitive, so a reordered array does not read as a change:
  ```sql
  SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT jsonb_array_elements(prev) EXCEPT SELECT jsonb_array_elements(cur)) x;  -- and the reverse
  ```
  Before concluding a key is absent, ask what keys exist: `SELECT jsonb_object_keys(data) FROM site_specs WHERE …`. And before attributing a count change to a page, **read `newest_component_update` against the item's `created_at`** — a component older than the filing cannot be what moved today's number.
- **and check the fleet-wide set too.** `claims_global.go` holds a **compile-time** banned-claim set joined at scan time and never persisted into any site's register, so a count can also move on a **roll** with neither the page nor `site_specs` changing. Three possible causes, two of them invisible in the site's own row.
- **source:** 2026-08-15, bugfix_168 lane, reading the daily revalidation sweep. Found because five items had counts captured before *and* after the same run and exactly one moved; the register diff that explains it took three attempts, the first two of which said "unchanged".
- **relations:** MEMORY [[a-model-upgrade-can-invert-a-closed-bugs-premise]] (a premise expires under you) · [[grep-the-config-key-before-calling-it-a-win.md]] · the `bugfix 161` entry — *correcting the register does not arm detection; `banned_claims` does* — this is the same seam read from the measurement side · the timing entry immediately above (both are "the reading is right, the frame is wrong")
- **added:** 2026-08-15, bugfix_168 deployed_asset_path lane

### `pages.name` is NOT the repo path — and `git log` on a path that never existed prints nothing at exit 0, which is what "unchanged" looks like

- **footprint:** `~/projects/sites/<domain>/**.html`, `pages.name` / `pages.url` on any ported site, `git log --since=… -- <path>`, `git show <ref>:<path>`, the per-page staleness check in `loanandmortgagecalculator_couk/HANDOFF_2026-08-14_continue_here.md` §3.1 and §7, `decompose_lmc.py` (`page_paths`, `assert_pin_matches_live`), `b2_verify.py` (`src()`)
- **fires when:** you check whether a page has changed since some date — before restoring from a dated backup, before trusting a pin, before reusing a golden. No symptom: an unchanged file and a misspelled path both print **nothing** and exit **0**.
- **the trap:** `pages.name` is the repo path with the **FIRST** slash replaced by a hyphen — `loans-damage-checker` ⇄ `loans/damage-checker.html`, `mortgages-rate-forecaster` ⇄ `mortgages/rate-forecaster.html`. Both files exist and both names are plausible, so pasting `pages.name` into a path builds `loanandmortgagecalculator.co.uk/loans-damage-checker.html`, which has **never existed in the repo**. `git log -- <that>` prints nothing and exits 0. The lane's own §7 tells you to read exactly this output as "empty ⇒ the backup is still valid for that page", so the false absence lands directly on a **restore** decision — and restoring from a stale backup on this site is the documented time machine that reverted a live `bugs_open/224` arithmetic fix for two days.
- **measured 2026-08-15:** all five mixed-card pages returned "0 commits since 2026-08-05", which I recorded as "the backup is safe for all five". Re-run against the real paths: **4 of the 5 had changed** — the 224 stale-answer guards and the btn-id fix — so the backup was stale for four of the five and the reading was not merely imprecise, it was inverted.
- **the check, and it is one line before the one you care about** — prove the path resolves, and run a control you know is wrong so an empty result cannot pass for an answer:
  ```bash
  git cat-file -e "$REF:$SITE/$REL" || echo "PATH DOES NOT EXIST — the git log below is meaningless"
  git log --oneline --since=2026-08-05 "$REF" -- "$SITE/$REL"
  # control: this MUST report missing. If it does not, your path builder is wrong.
  git cat-file -e "$REF:$SITE/${REL//\//-}" 2>/dev/null && echo "UNEXPECTED"
  ```
  Or derive the path from the repo rather than from the DB name: `git ls-tree -r --name-only <ref> -- <site>/ | grep <stem>`, which cannot name a file that is not there. `pages.url` already holds the real relative path (`/loans/damage-checker.html`) — prefer it to reconstructing one from `name`.
- **why a set-comparison would not have saved you:** the site has 41 pages and 52 repo files; a count check on either side is unchanged by asking about a file that does not exist. Only resolving the individual path discriminates.
- **source:** 2026-08-15, loanandmortgagecalculator Track B2 batch 2, checking the mixed-card five against the 08-05 backup before seeding. Found only because 0-for-5 looked too convenient to be true.
- **relations:** the entry above on **a restore from a dated backup is a TIME MACHINE** — this is the check that feeds that decision, and it is the one that failed · MEMORY [[measurement-discipline-index]] (*a grep proves absence only for the SPELLING it searches*) · [[a-post-fix-zero-needs-a-demand-control]] (an empty result needs a control that could have come out non-empty)
- **added:** 2026-08-15, loanandmortgagecalculator B2 mixed-card thread

### Adding a section to a `rebuild_policy='owned'` page: BOTH sanctioned actions refuse, and the site's own tool pages will tell you it is impossible

- **footprint:** `pages.rebuild_policy='owned'`, `platform/orchestration/actions/save_page_sections_action.go:186-196`, `owned_page_guard.go:29-36`, `apply_section_edit` / `ApplySectionEditInputSpec` (`section_editor_actions.go:46-60`), `docs/agent_docs/sql_for_agents/267_tool_guide_intro_recovery_waterfall.sql`, `docs/agent_docs/docs024_key_docs_latest/cta_link_integrity/scripts/049b_deploy_single_page.sh`, any `tool-*` page
- **fires when:** you need to ADD a component to an existing tool/widget page — merging prose onto a tool page, adding a guide intro, giving a calculator an explainer. No symptom first: you go looking for the action, find two that sound right, and both say no.
- **the trap, in three parts:**
  1. **`SavePageSectionsAction` HARD-REFUSES an owned page** — its DELETE-and-reinsert is the TL-001 clobber. Its error names two alternatives ("apply_section_edit for targeted edits or the tool pipeline for rebuilds"), and **neither of them can add a section**.
  2. **`apply_section_edit` only edits an EXISTING `page_components` row.** Both its edit types (`content_edit`, `component_swap`) target a `page_component_id`. There is no add.
  3. **So the honest conclusion from the actions alone is "the platform cannot do this" — and that is WRONG.** `owned_page_guard.go:29-36` states the design: the guard sits at `assemble_page` precisely because re-assembly of existing `page_components` "is deliberately NOT gated — it is how owned pages deploy". A direct INSERT plus an **assemble-only** deploy is the sanctioned route, not a workaround. Worked precedent: `267_tool_guide_intro_recovery_waterfall.sql`.
- **⚠ THE MEASUREMENT THAT LOOKS DECISIVE AND POINTS THE WRONG WAY.** A site's own tool pages are usually single-component, so "tool pages here don't carry prose" reads as a settled convention. **[MEASURED 2026-08-15, fleet-wide] 23 active `owned` pages carry >1 component** — 9 on loanandmortgagecalculator.co.uk with a deliberate `prose-0 / tool-1 / prose-2` interleave, plus `oufe.com tool-recovery-waterfall` and `webdesign.co.uk tool-ab-test-calculator`. robot-hands' three `tool-` pages are all single-component, i.e. **the local n=3 says the opposite of the fleet**. Ask the fleet, not the site:
  ```sql
  SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT p.id FROM pages p JOIN page_components pc ON pc.page_id=p.id
    WHERE COALESCE(p.rebuild_policy,'generic')='owned' AND p.status='active'
    GROUP BY p.id HAVING count(pc.id)>1) t;   -- 23 on 2026-08-15, not 0
  ```
- **the check, before ANY assemble-only deploy of a page you have just added rows to** — `049b_deploy_single_page.sh`'s own header warns that **if ANY section has NULL `content_data` the whole page escalates to the content writer and the copy IS regenerated.** On a tool page **that regenerates the tool**. NULL and `'{}'` are not the same thing and only one of them is safe:
  ```sql
  SELECT slot_name, content_data IS NULL AS is_null, content_data->>'deploy_mode' AS mode
    FROM page_components WHERE page_id='<page>';
  -- is_null must be false on EVERY row. mode='verbatim' + exactly 1 component means the
  -- page is on the verbatim-serve path (rerender_single_page_action.go:287-311) and
  -- attaching a second component changes its serving mode — intended, but know it.
  ```
  And pass **no 4th argument** to `049b`: a reason takes the `rerender_sections` pre-pass instead of assemble-only.
- **two things worth copying from 267 and two worth NOT copying.** Copy: `NOT EXISTS` replay guard on `(page_id, slot_name)`, and write `rendered_html` in the same statement. Do **not** blindly copy its `pages.sections` append (assembly reads `page_components ORDER BY position ASC`, never that column — and writing it flips `ensure_page_section_layout_action.go:118` from "will write a layout" to "refuses, already non-empty"), nor its `lock_type='permanent'` unless the copy is genuinely hand-authored — locking framework-written content opts it out of ordinary maintenance for no gain.
- **source:** 2026-08-15, `bugs_open/215` O2 pair 7 (robot-hands `gripper-cycle-time-estimator`). The lane's own handoff said the merge needed "~1,700 words the framework must write"; the words were two finished deployed components and moved verbatim. The fleet-wide query above is the one that saved it, and it was run specifically to disconfirm the n=3 reading.
- **relations:** MEMORY [[measurement-discipline-index]] (*your measurement answers the question you ENCODED*) · [[a-post-fix-zero-needs-a-demand-control]] (a zero needs a control that could have come out otherwise) · [[shared-actions-are-estate-design-not-a-smell]] · the `bugfix 117` chrome entry (stored artefacts that no rerender regenerates)
- **added:** 2026-08-15, brochure_215_o2_thread

### Writing ANYTHING to `site_work_items.result` on an open row postpones the stale reaper for ever, and the row looks perfectly healthy while it happens

- **footprint:** `site_work_items.result`, `site_work_items.updated_at`, `trg_site_work_items_updated_at`, `scheduled_tasks` row `stale-work-item-reaper`, `docs/agent_docs/sql_for_agents/237_stale_reaper_keys_on_time_in_triaged.sql`, `platform/orchestration/actions/write_audit_findings_retraction.go` (`workItemInFlightStatuses`), `resolveWorkItems`
- **fires when:** you add ANY periodic bookkeeping write to an open work item — a retry counter, a last-seen stamp, a silence streak, a "we looked at this again" marker. No symptom first: your write succeeds, the column holds what you meant, and every test passes.
- **the trap:** `site_work_items` carries exactly one non-internal trigger, `trg_site_work_items_updated_at` (BEFORE UPDATE), so **`updated_at` is bumped by ANY write to the row and no careful column list can avoid it** — you cannot opt out by not naming the column. Meanwhile the live `stale-work-item-reaper` (enabled, hourly) parks wedged items with `status='triaged' AND pipeline='build' AND updated_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '48 hours' AND claimed_at IS NULL`. **A bookkeeping write on any cadence faster than 48h makes every `triaged` row it touches permanently unreapable** — which is the queue deadlock that reaper exists to prevent. Migration `237`'s own header predicted this in the abstract ("anything that touches the row for unrelated reasons bumps `updated_at` and postpones reaping") and it was written as a *stated risk of that migration*, not as a warning to future writers, so nobody touching `result` ever reads it. **Sharpened 2026-08-21 (344 lane's round): "periodic" is the sufficient framing, not the necessary one — the reaper reads only `updated_at`, so a SINGLE write postpones a reap by up to 48h, and the cadence that decides "for ever" is the ROW'S aggregate write rate across ALL writers, not any one writer's intent. Five independent "one-off" writers each landing under 48h apart are a periodic writer in effect, and each of the five tests as harmless alone.**
- **why nothing prompts you to check:** the damage is an ABSENCE — a park that never happens. There is no error, no failed write, no changed value to inspect; the row simply stays `triaged` for ever, looking exactly like a row that is fine. And the population is invisible on a healthy day: [MEASURED 2026-07-27, and it is why the migration could not be tested] there is essentially no `triaged` build backlog at any moment, because the claimer drains it in ~2 minutes.
- **the check, BEFORE you add the write — enumerate the readers, do not assume there is one:**
  ```sql
  -- Which scheduled tasks actually read site_work_items.updated_at?
  SELECT name, enabled, (pre_query ILIKE '%updated_at%') AS reads_updated_at
  FROM scheduled_tasks WHERE pre_query ILIKE '%site_work_items%'
  ORDER BY enabled DESC, name;
  -- 2026-08-15: three match the LIKE and only ONE genuinely reads this column.
  -- claimed-item-timeout keys on claimed_at and orchestration_states.updated_at;
  -- improvement-sweep reads sites.updated_at. Read the pre_query, not the LIKE.
  SELECT tgname FROM pg_trigger t JOIN pg_class c ON c.oid=t.tgrelid
  WHERE c.relname='site_work_items' AND NOT tgisinternal;   -- proves you cannot avoid the bump
  ```
- **the remedy, and it is a status exclusion rather than a column trick:** exclude the statuses a reaper watches from whatever you are writing to. `workItemInFlightStatuses` = {`triaged`, `claimed`} is the live example. It costs almost nothing here (a `triaged` row is claimed within ~2 minutes) and it is the ONLY protection available, because the trigger removes every other one. **Anyone widening such a set must re-run the enumeration above first** — the reader list is config, not code, so it can change without a commit.
- **⚠ the near-miss that is the real lesson:** the two reasons for excluding those statuses are NOT equal. "The pipeline is actively carrying the item" is a judgement someone can reasonably talk you out of; "the reaper keys on this column and the trigger bumps it" is mechanical and cannot be argued with. **Write the mechanical reason down as the load-bearing one**, or the next reader relaxes the rule on the strength of the softer one.
- **source:** 2026-08-15, `bugfix_213_verifier_producer_join` D1 half two (`WII-018`). Found while designing a silence-streak counter that would have written to open `dark_section_audit` rows every 900s. It was caught by grepping for readers of `updated_at` before writing the UPDATE, not by any test — no unit test can see a scheduled task's `pre_query`.
- **relations:** MEMORY [[your-action-moves-you-to-the-back-of-the-selector]] (*filing your finding bumps `updated_at` and sorts it to the back* — same column, same class, opposite direction) · [[declaring-a-key-silences-your-own-detector]] · the `WII-018` register entry carries the same landmine attached to the mechanism

### A mutation test can pass because the MOCK refused the call, not because your guard did — and that reads as a proven guard

- **footprint:** `github.com/DATA-DOG/go-sqlmock`, any `*_test.go` asserting that something does NOT happen, `mock.ExpectationsWereMet`, `platform/orchestration/actions/write_audit_findings_retraction_test.go`
- **fires when:** you write the natural test for a guard that prevents work — "set no `ExpectBegin`, run it, assert no result came back". No symptom first: the test passes, it passes for the right-looking reason, and it keeps passing after you delete the guard.
- **the trap:** with the guard removed the code DOES call the database. sqlmock refuses the unexpected call and returns an error; the caller logs the error and returns its no-op result; **your assertion is satisfied by the mock's refusal instead of by the code's guard.** Both worlds produce an identical pass. sqlmock cannot express "this call must not happen" either — setting an expectation you intend not to be met fails `ExpectationsWereMet`, so the obvious fix is unavailable.
- **the check:** **test the FUNCTION, not the action.** Call the guarded function directly with a mock that has NO expectations at all, and assert on its ERROR RETURN — then a stray database call becomes a failure the assertion can actually see, because nothing upstream swallows it into a log line. Pair it with the opposite-direction test (the case that SHOULD reach the database) so "guard always on" is caught too; one test alone cannot distinguish a working guard from a dead code path.
- **how it was found, which is the point:** not by review. The mutation matrix removed the guard and the test stayed GREEN. **A guard whose removal changes no test verdict is not proven, however carefully the test was written** — and this one had been written carefully, by someone who had just written five other tests in the same file that all discriminated properly.
- **the sibling result from the same run, worth knowing before you conclude your own guard is dead:** a mutation that passes may have hit a **guard in series**. Removing the first of two short-circuit returns failed nothing because the second one caught it; the property was only detectable when both went. Before deleting a guard your matrix says is untested, check whether something behind it is doing the work — and prefer passing the real condition down to a shared helper over short-circuiting above it, so each guard can be mutated one at a time.
- **and the third result, on what to do when a mutation genuinely is not caught:** one of ours was unreachable by construction (an inner re-check the outer scope already guaranteed). **It was DELETED, not kept and not given a test.** Untested defence reads as protection and is not, and a test written to justify unreachable code proves only that you can reach it from a test.
- **source:** 2026-08-15, `bugfix_213_verifier_producer_join` D1 half two. 9 mutations run, gated on exit status with an unmutated control and a byte-identity check afterwards; 8 caught, and all three lessons above came out of the one that was not.
- **relations:** MEMORY [[mutate-the-code-to-prove-the-guard]] (*a mock's own bookkeeping cannot assert a NEGATIVE*) · [[a-mutation-that-passes-may-have-hit-a-guard-in-series]] · [[a-helper-with-no-callers-is-not-a-refactor]] · `WRONG_CALLS.md` 2026-08-15 entry
- **added:** 2026-08-15, bugfix_213_verifier_producer_join lane

### A concept-register entry can be corrected in ONE bullet and left false in another — and the stale half is the one people quote

- **footprint:** `docs/agent_docs/docs026_concept_register/register/`, `LCO-008`, `platform/aiservice/anthropic.go` (`cacheTTL`, `CacheBreakpointMarker`), any register entry carrying a `council verdict` bullet
- **fires when:** you read a register entry's `what:` line to learn what a mechanism does. The estate already has an entry for *"a register STATUS line is a snapshot that outlives its truth"*; this is the sharper version — **the entry does not have to be uniformly stale to mislead. It can be internally contradictory, with the correction present and the headline wrong.**
- **the worked case, measured 2026-08-15.** `LCO-008` (prompt caching) described the mechanism as sending `cache_control ephemeral, ttl 1h`. It never did. The council removed `ttl:"1h"` before the code shipped, and the entry recorded that removal accurately — **in a nested bullet nine lines further down**, under the council-verdict trail. The `what:` line was never updated. So for five days the entry simultaneously asserted an hour (in the line a reader reaches first) and no-ttl-at-all (in the line a reader reaches if they get that far), while production ran the 5-minute default.
- **why it is worse than an ordinary stale entry:** council seats read this register as ground truth, and the `what:` line is the part a seat quotes. A reviewer checking "does this client already use an extended TTL?" would have been told yes by the authoritative-looking line and no by the archaeology. Neither is flagged; both look deliberate.
- **the check:** when a council verdict changes what actually shipped, **grep the whole entry for the thing that changed and fix every occurrence** — not just the bullet you are writing. `grep -n "ttl\|TTL" <entry>` would have taken one second and shown two answers. And when reading: if an entry has a `council verdict` bullet, read it BEFORE trusting the `what:` line, because the verdict is where the `what:` gets contradicted.
- **the general form:** the ordering of a register entry is adversarial to this failure — `what:` is written first and rarely revisited, while verdicts and corrections accrete at the bottom. Assume the top of a long entry is the oldest text in it.
- **added:** 2026-08-15, bugfix_209/231 lane, found while flipping `cacheTTL` to `1h` and discovering the entry had been describing the destination rather than the state

## A config-backed fix ships in TWO halves — the build stamp proves the binary and says nothing about the migration, and the binary degrades SILENTLY

- **footprint:** `internal/adapters/thunder/store/config.go` (`LoadConfig`) · `thunder_config.provision_wait_timeout_seconds` · any `store.LoadConfig`-style read using `(to_jsonb(t)->>'col')::int` · `scripts/migration/run-migrations.sh` · every "is my fix live?" check based on `build provenance` + `git merge-base`
- **fires when:** you ship a fix whose behaviour depends on a new config column, verify it the estate's approved way — read the running service's `build provenance` stamp, confirm your commit is an ancestor — and conclude the fix is live. **The stamp only proves the binary half.** If the migration has not been applied, the code takes its fallback path and the old behaviour continues.
- **why the wrong result looks exactly right:** the fallback is *deliberate and correct* — degrading to a compiled-in default is what stops an unmigrated database breaking every call (which is why the read uses `to_jsonb`, so a missing column is NULL rather than an error). So nothing fails, nothing logs an error, and the ancestry check genuinely passes. **Measured here: 44 hours** between `v1.0.1295` shipping `bugs_open/258` defect 2's fix and migration 400 being applied — during which the adapter used the hardcoded 5-minute deadline the fix existed to remove, while every deploy check said "shipped".
- **the check — assert the VALUE, not the version:**
  ```sql
  -- 1. does the column exist at all?
  SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.columns
  WHERE table_name='thunder_config' AND column_name='provision_wait_timeout_seconds';
  -- 2. run the EXACT projection the code runs, and read the value back
  SELECT (to_jsonb(t)->>'provision_wait_timeout_seconds')::int FROM thunder_config t LIMIT 1;
  -- 3. and confirm the migration is RECORDED, not merely applied by hand
  SELECT filename FROM schema_migrations WHERE filename LIKE '400_%';
  ```
  At the service, the fallback names itself — this WARN is the whole tell:
  `provision_wait_timeout_seconds not available — using compiled-in default (is migration 400 applied?)`
- **so: make the fallback SAY SO.** A silent default is indistinguishable from a configured one. If you write a `resolveX(cfg)` helper with a compiled-in fallback, log at WARN naming the migration — it costs one line and it is the only thing standing between "degraded safely" and "quietly did nothing".
- **the general rule:** *"prove it at the artefact"* has two artefacts for a config-backed change — **the binary AND the row**. A deploy check that reads only the stamp answers "is the code there", never "is the behaviour on".
- **relations:** the `prove-a-deploy-at-the-artefact` family (this is its config-shaped blind spot) · `bugs_open/258` defect 2 · FTW-044 · the ordering note in migration 400's header (396 was the opposite case — there the adapter treats an absent table as a HARD ERROR and refuses to provision, deliberately, because that one is a safety guard rather than a tunable)
- **source:** 2026-08-15, `finetuning_uk_service` lane. Found by checking whether the column existed *after* confirming the commit was in the running build — the ancestry check had already said "live", and it was right and insufficient.
- **added:** 2026-08-15, finetuning_uk_service lane

### `oracle.py --mutate expectation` reporting CONTROL OK does NOT mean every check is guarded — it cannot test a text assertion at all, and it has cried wolf twice

- **footprint:** `loanandmortgagecalculator_couk/oracle.py` (`run_case`, the `raw_contains` branch and the `want = 100.0` sentinel), `oracle.py --mutate expectation`, `--mutate crosstool`, `chk(raw_contains=…)`, any batch gate whose closing evidence is "the mutation control passed"
- **fires when:** you close a batch on this lane's mandatory gate, or you read a past session's "controls fired in-session" as meaning the whole suite was exercised. No symptom either way: the control prints `CONTROL OK` whether or not the checks it cannot reach are working.
- **the trap, two independent halves:**
  - **A `raw_contains` check is structurally invisible to the control.** It asserts TEXT ("Option A is Cheaper", "2 Years 3 Months"); the branch returns **before** the numeric mutation is applied, so no corruption of an expectation can move it. Counting those as PASS made the control announce *"8 checks PASSED … the checker is inert"* on a checker that was working correctly.
  - **The sentinel can be a real answer.** The mutation asserts `100.0`, commented as *"a number nothing computes"* — false for any vector built to sit on that boundary. `inv(400000, 1200, 300000, 300000, "asymmetric; LTV exactly 100%")` has loan == value, so its LTV genuinely is 100.0%.
- **why it is worse than an ordinary gap:** both halves fail **toward the alarm**, and this file's own docstring already records the same shape once before (2026-08-12, determinism checks) with the note that **a control that cries wolf gets ignored**. It had already blocked a Track B page once. The next session to meet a spurious "the checker is inert" is measurably more likely to wave it through — which is the one thing a last-line control cannot afford.
- **the check, when the control accuses the checker:** **list the passing checks before believing either story** — `python3 oracle.py --mutate expectation --json out.json`, then print every `status == "PASS"` with its page and `what`. If they are text assertions, or their true expectation equals the sentinel, the control is wrong and the checker is fine. And when you fix it, **prove both directions in the same session**: the normal sweep must be unchanged (it shares the branch) and the arithmetic must close exactly — 7 pre-existing N/A + 8 newly excluded = 15, not merely "fewer passes than before".
- **⚠ AND DO NOT EXCLUDE THE SAME CHECK FROM BOTH CONTROLS — THE TWO ARE NOT ALIKE.** My first fix did, and a second session on the lane caught it the same day. `expectation` corrupts `want` at a line the `raw_contains` branch **never reaches**, so a text check is immune *by construction* and the exclusion is forced. `crosstool` swaps in the **donor's whole check dict, `raw_contains` included**, so a text check IS genuinely mis-paired and MUST fail. Measured across three versions: `FAIL 154` before, **`FAIL 148` under the blanket exclusion — 6 real comparisons silenced** (compare-loans' four verdicts alternate Option A/B between adjacent vectors; two of overpayment's three prose readings) — `FAIL 154` after narrowing it to a borrowed==own STRING guard. **"It looks parallel to the determinism exclusion" is exactly the reasoning that fails here.**
- **THE RESIDUALS, and they are NOT fixed:**
  - the expectation mutation only ever tested the ~161 checks that compare a parsed NUMBER. **No control in this file can test a `raw_contains` check under `--mutate expectation`**, so one that has silently stopped matching would not be caught there. Do not read `CONTROL OK` as coverage of those 7.
  - ~~**`--mutate crosstool` STILL EXITS 1** … `_true_want` comes back `None` so the float NON-TEST guard cannot fire …~~ **THAT MECHANISM WAS WRONG AND I PUBLISHED IT. CORRECTED 2026-08-15 (`a848812cd`, peer session).** Crosstool is now **FIXED** — PASS 0 / FAIL 154 / N/A 13, exit 0, with FAIL pinned so nothing was silenced. The real cause: **the NON-TEST guards tested `isinstance(tw, float)` and were type-blind to INTS.** All three `_true_want` values were present and equal to the borrowed one, and all three were ints (consolidation 5000, bridging 200000, overpayment 2), so the guard that exists for exactly this could never fire. Fixed with a `numeric()` helper (int or float, bool excluded) at all three guard sites. **Every tool's vectors carry identical selector sequences — measured — so no `None` `_true_want` exists anywhere in the suite** and the different-length-vector story described something that does not happen.
  - **⚠ HOW I GOT IT WRONG, because the method is the transferable part:** I dumped the control's JSON and printed `r.get("_true_want")` per row. It read `None` on all three — and `_true_want` is **never written into the result record at all** (it lives on the check dict; `rec` never receives it). I read the absence of a key as the value of a field and built a mechanism on it. **A `.get()` on a key that was never in the schema returns exactly what a real `None` returns.** Print the keys the record actually has before attributing meaning to a missing one.
- **source:** 2026-08-15, loanandmortgagecalculator Track B2 batch 2, closing gate. Fixed in `b40d7d982`; measurements in `NOTES_…md` 2026-08-15 (c).
- **relations:** MEMORY [[a-pass-from-a-blind-check-outlives-the-blindness]] (closed files later quote it as "verified") · [[a-post-fix-zero-needs-a-demand-control]] · [[mutate-the-code-to-prove-the-guard]] · [[a-quiet-test-passes-when-the-rule-is-gone]]
- **added:** 2026-08-15, loanandmortgagecalculator B2 mixed-card thread

### `075_trigger_discovery.sh <domain>` ignores your domain at the end and TRIAGES `finetuning.uk`'s items — a read-only-looking "trigger discovery" dispatches real repairs at a site you never named

- **footprint:** `scripts/initial_messages/170_work_item_flow_build/075_trigger_discovery.sh`, and by shape any `initial_messages` trigger whose tail contains follow-up `psql` calls
- **fires when:** you want to exercise a discovery/audit path at some site and reach for the obviously-named shipped script. No symptom: it prints a correlation id and a tidy "Discovery triggered" banner exactly as it would on success.
- **the trap, three independent halves:**
  - **Lines 79–91 are hardcoded to `finetuning.uk`**, ignoring `$DOMAIN` entirely. The last one is not a query — it is `UPDATE site_work_items SET status='triaged' … WHERE site_id=(SELECT id FROM sites WHERE domain='finetuning.uk') AND status='detected'`. **`triaged` is exactly the predicate `build-pipeline-trigger` claims on** (enabled, 60s tick), so this promotes another site's suggestions into instructions and the repair fleet acts on them. You asked to *look* at site X and you *edited* site Y.
  - It publishes with the **`kubectl run -i --rm … kcat -P <<JSON` heredoc form**, which drops ~4 of 5 publishes at exit 0 — so the half that was supposed to happen often does not, while the half that was not supposed to happen always does.
  - `set -euo pipefail` with an unguarded `case "$2"` at line 17 means its **own documented one-argument usage (`./075_trigger_discovery.sh finetuning.uk`) crashes** under `-u`, which is a fair hint the tail has not been exercised in a long time.
- **the check, before running ANY `initial_messages` trigger:** read to the END of the file, not just the usage header — `sed -n '/kcat/,$p' <script>`. A trigger that ends after the publish is a trigger; one with `psql` after it is a small program with side effects, and the domain it acts on may not be the one you passed. If you only want the dispatch, lift the publish block out and run that.
- **the safe form of what it was trying to do:** `RUNBOOK_verifier_producer_join.md` §9 — dispatch the producing agent directly, payload in the container COMMAND with a `PUBLISH_OK` receipt, and let findings sit at `detected` (inert) instead of triaging them.
- **source:** 2026-08-15, `bugfix_213` lane, while looking for a way to exercise WII-018 without re-enabling `improvement-sweep`. Caught by reading the script before running it; nothing about its name or banner would have told me afterwards.
- **relations:** MEMORY [[kcat-publish-silently-drops]] (the publish half) · [[operator-actions-that-email-a-human]] (same shape: one button, two effects, only one of them named) · [[live-and-committed-are-independent-facts]]
- **added:** 2026-08-15, bugfix_213 lane

### Enabling a `scheduled_tasks` row proves nothing — a task whose `pre_query` selects 0 rows fires, dispatches nothing, and is indistinguishable from a clean run

- **footprint:** `scheduled_tasks` (`enabled`, `pre_query`, `last_triggered_at`), `site-discovery-rotation-*`, `improvement-sweep`, any "switch it on briefly to test it" plan
- **fires when:** you flip `enabled=true` to exercise a code path, then read `last_triggered_at` advancing as evidence it ran. It did fire — the scheduler updates that column regardless — but the `pre_query` returned no rows, so nothing was dispatched and no agent ever executed.
- **the trap:** these `pre_query` bodies carry recency predicates (`last_selected_at < now() - interval '7 days'`, `updated_at ASC LIMIT 1`) that go **empty precisely because the task has been off**, or because a sibling task already consumed the due set. Measured 2026-08-15: `site-discovery-rotation-design` selected **0 rows** — oldest live stamp 6d04h against a 7-day threshold — so enabling it would have produced a fired task, an advanced timestamp, and zero work.
- **the check, and it is read-only:** **run the `pre_query`'s SELECT half yourself before flipping anything.** `SELECT pre_query FROM scheduled_tasks WHERE name='<task>';` then execute it — but ⚠ **strip any write first**: several of these are CTEs that `INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` a rotation stamp as a side effect of being read, so pasting one verbatim consumes the very due-ness you are testing. Zero rows → the switch is not your lever, and no amount of waiting will change that.
- **the better lever:** dispatch the target agent directly (RUNBOOK §9 pattern) — you pick the row, nothing depends on a recency predicate, and you avoid whatever *else* the task does. Check that too: `improvement-sweep` reads as a detection sweep and its description ends "**dispatch fixes them**".
- **source:** 2026-08-15, `bugfix_213` lane. The plan was "enable the safe-looking carrier for one tick"; the carrier was both inert AND not a carrier of that code at all.
- **relations:** MEMORY [[zero-adoption-means-read-the-mechanism]] (a silent mechanism is usually undriven) · [[detection-works-schedule-and-dispatch-do-not]] · [[a-post-fix-zero-needs-a-demand-control]] (a zero needs a control proving demand existed)
- **added:** 2026-08-15, bugfix_213 lane

### `visual-design-auditor` returns OPPOSITE verdicts on a byte-identical page — ONE audit result is a sample, not a measurement of the page, and an ABSENT finding is the unreliable direction

- **footprint:** `visual-design-auditor`, `design-audit-agent`, `write_audit_findings`, `classification_stats`, `site_work_items.item_type='dark_section_audit'`, any "the audit no longer reports X, so X is fixed" claim
- **fires when:** you run an audit (or read one run's findings) and treat the output as the state of the page — to confirm a repair landed, to close a ticket, to populate a before/after, or to decide a finding was a false positive because a later run did not repeat it. No symptom: both runs complete, both return a full well-formed findings list, and neither reports any error.
- **the trap, measured 2026-08-15 with everything else held still:** two runs against `mortgagecalculator.co.uk` **40 minutes apart** returned 5 findings each. The first classified **no** `dark_section_audit`; the second classified one (`--hero-btn-ink`). The page was **byte-identical** across both (`curl` before and after, 36,807 bytes, `cmp -s` clean), **nothing repaired it in between** (no `site_work_items` row on that site changed between the audits except the second run's own), and **the defect the second run found was present in the copy fetched before it ran** (`--hero-btn-ink` × 3).
