- **verifier note 2026-08-17:** the landmine-verifier returned **UNVERIFIABLE** on this entry, and **that is not doubt about it** — the verifier reads the Go code index, which covers only `.go` files, so a makefile-footprinted entry is outside what it can see (the neighbouring `IMAGE_TAG`/`imagePullPolicy` entry drew `NEEDS_HUMAN_REVIEW` the same afternoon for the same reason). Verified by hand instead, on this tree: `make -n release | grep -c render-audit-adapter` → **0**, while `make -n deploy-agents | grep -c render-audit-adapter` → **non-zero** and the pod runs `browser-runner-adapter:v1.0.1305`. **Any landmine whose footprint is a makefile, a manifest or SQL needs a hand-run check written into the entry, because the automated one cannot grade it.**

### `orchestration_states.owner_agent_type` is NOT "which agent ran" — it reads ZERO for a demonstrably active agent, and a dormancy claim built on it inverts a bug's severity

- **footprint:** `orchestration_states.owner_agent_type` · `llm_call_log.agent_type` · `site_work_items.handler_agent` · any "is this agent dormant / has this ever run / is this a live burn" question · `bugs_open/297`, `bugs_open/298`, `bugs_open/257` §4
- **fires when:** you are sizing a defect and need to know whether the agent that carries it actually runs — the difference between "a live burn" and "a latent cleanup", which is usually the whole severity argument. The obvious query is `SELECT count(*) FROM orchestration_states WHERE owner_agent_type='<agent>'`, and it is the wrong instrument.
- **the tell — a confident ZERO for an agent that is plainly working.** Measured 2026-08-17: `owner_agent_type='tool-recreation-handler'` → **0 orchestrations**, while `llm_call_log` for the same `agent_type` holds **290 calls, most recent 2026-08-11**, and `site_work_items.handler_agent` names it on 4 items. Same run: `owner_agent_type='internal-linker'` → 0, while 69 work items name it as handler with the newest dated **that same day**. The column carries the ORCHESTRATION's owner, which for a handler dispatched into a loop is the *parent* workflow, not the handler. A zero here is "this agent did not own a top-level run", which is not the question you asked.
- **why it is dangerous rather than merely wrong:** it fails toward "dormant", and dormant is the answer that makes a bug go away. Had I trusted it, `bugs_open/297` would have been filed as a latent cleanup on an idle agent; it is in fact live and bites at 19 of 24 sites.
- **the check, and use TWO because each has a blind spot:**
  ```sql
  SELECT agent_type, count(*), max(created_at) FROM llm_call_log WHERE agent_type='<agent>' GROUP BY 1;
  SELECT status, count(*), max(created_at) FROM site_work_items WHERE handler_agent='<agent>' GROUP BY 1;
  ```
  `llm_call_log` is blind to an agent with no LLM step, or one whose LLM step is never reached (`bugs_open/298`: 69 dispatched items, 0 LLM rows). `handler_agent` is blind to an agent driven by a schedule rather than by work items. **Agreeing zeros are evidence; one zero is not.** And if both read zero while a definition is `is_active`, that is a finding in itself (`bugs_open/257`: a deployed service consuming a topic nothing publishes to) — not a licence to call the bug latent.
- **source:** `bugfix_275_silent_row_caps` lane, 2026-08-17, while filing `bugs_open/297`/`298`; the same shape appears in `bugs_open/257` §4, where `llm_call_log` was the blind instrument and the POD log was the honest one
- **added:** 2026-08-17, bugfix_275_silent_row_caps lane

### Two live agents whose names differ by one word — `internal-linker` vs `internal-link-resolver` — and the busy one is not the one carrying your defect

- **footprint:** `agent_definitions.type` · `internal-linker` / `internal-link-resolver` · `tool-suggester` / `tool-generator` / `tool-recreation-handler` / `tool-improver` / `tool-auditor` · any measurement attributed to "the linker" or "the tool agent" · `bugs_open/298`
- **fires when:** you measure activity for an agent by a name you typed from memory or from a bug file, and a *different* agent with a near-identical name absorbs the traffic. Nothing errors: both names exist, both are `is_active`, and each returns a plausible number.
- **the tell:** the numbers are plausible but attached to the wrong subject. Measured 2026-08-17: `internal-link-resolver` has **54 orchestrations and NO capped query at all**; `internal-linker` has **0 orchestrations, 69 work items, and the `LIMIT 15` the bug is about**. Reading the first and concluding about the second gives you "busy agent, capped query" — a live burn that does not exist. The `tool-*` family is the same hazard at five members.
- **the check, before attributing ANY measurement:** enumerate the near-neighbours first, and read the workflow, not the name —
  ```sql
  SELECT type, is_active, created_at::date FROM agent_definitions
   WHERE type LIKE '%link%' AND COALESCE(is_snapshot,false)=false AND deleted_at IS NULL;
  SELECT s.key, s.value->>'action' FROM agent_definitions a,
         LATERAL jsonb_each(a.default_config->'workflow'->'steps') s
   WHERE a.type='<the exact one>' ORDER BY 1;
  ```
  **The step list is the identity.** If the agent you are writing about does not contain the step your bug is about, you have the wrong agent — which is a one-query check and the only one that cannot be fooled by a plausible name.
- **source:** `bugfix_275_silent_row_caps` lane, 2026-08-17, caught while filing `bugs_open/298` — `owner_agent_type` returned `internal-link-resolver` for a query about `internal-linker`, which is what exposed both this and the entry above
- **added:** 2026-08-17, bugfix_275_silent_row_caps lane

### `site_work_items.status` has TWO terminal SUCCESS states — a success-rate or "has it ever worked?" test that counts only `complete` gets WORSE as the platform verifies more work

- **footprint:** `site_work_items.status` · `complete_work_item_verification.go` · `idx_swi_completed` · `scheduled_tasks.detected-item-promoter` pre_query · migrations `430`, `444`, `454` · any handler-reliability, success-ratio or known-good gate
- **fires when:** you write `status='complete'` as the definition of "this handler worked". `complete_work_item_verification.go:218` writes **`status='verified'`** onto a row that completed *and then passed verification* — a success with **more** evidence behind it, not less. `idx_swi_completed`'s own predicate already says so: `WHERE status IN ('complete','verified','rejected','wont_fix')`.
- **why the wrong result looks exactly like the right one:** the number is correct at the instant you read it, and it moves *downward over time with no code change at all*. A pair measured at **11 complete / 13 failed = 46%** at 11:00Z read **3 complete / 12 failed = 20%** at 16:30Z — nothing regressed; a verification sweep had moved 9 completes to `verified`. Counting both, it is 12/12 = 50%. So a gate keyed on `complete` **penalises exactly the handlers whose work got checked**, and its verdicts silently drift as verification spreads.
- **the check, before you use the column as a success test:** enumerate the domain rather than assuming it — `SELECT status, count(*) FROM site_work_items GROUP BY 1;`. Then write successes as `status IN ('complete','verified')`. The latent form is worse than the visible one: a pair whose successes have **all** been verified has **zero** `complete` rows and reads as *never having worked*, which in the promoter's known-good rule means held for ever — the exact stranding `bugs_open/083` exists to cure.
- **scope when found (2026-08-17):** `verified` was rare — 9 rows, 1 pair — so exactly one pair changed verdict and no pair was yet in the latent zero-complete state. Caught while the population was small; it grows.
- **relation:** same table, same day, same family as *"`failed` rows carry NO `completed_at`"* — both are a **status column whose values were assumed instead of enumerated**, and in both cases the wrong answer is well-formed and plausible. If you are about to filter `site_work_items` on `status`, `GROUP BY status` first.
- **source:** 2026-08-17, `bugfix_277_required_fields_repair` lane, correcting its own migration `444` about four hours after applying it — found by noticing a pair's ratio had moved under it, not by review. WRONG_CALLS 2026-08-17c.
- **added:** 2026-08-17, bugfix_277/083 lane

### Running a `scheduled_tasks.pre_query` by hand to "see what it would pick" ADVANCES the rotation and costs a real site its turn

- **footprint:** `scheduled_tasks.pre_query` · `site_discovery_rotation` · `site-render-audit-rotation` · `site-discovery-rotation-availability` · any task whose `pre_query` contains `INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`ON CONFLICT` · `cmd/scheduler/main.go` `runPreQuery`
- **fires when:** you are debugging why a scheduled task did or did not fire, and you copy its `pre_query` out of the DB and run it to see what it returns. That is the obvious move and it looks completely read-only — the text *ends* in `SELECT sid::text, domain FROM due`, and what you get back is a `SELECT` result.
- **why the wrong result looks exactly like the right one:** these pre_queries are **CTE-shaped, with the state change hidden in the middle**. `site-render-audit-rotation`'s reads `WITH due AS (SELECT … LIMIT 1), stamped AS (INSERT INTO site_discovery_rotation … ON CONFLICT … DO UPDATE SET last_selected_at = now()) SELECT … FROM due`. **In Postgres a data-modifying CTE always executes to completion, whether or not the main query references it** — so your "look" writes `last_selected_at = now()` for the site it returned. The site then reads as freshly audited, drops out of the due set for another **7 days**, and the audit it was owed never happens. Nothing errors, nothing logs, and the row you were investigating is the one you just skipped.
- **the check, every time:** wrap it. `{ echo "BEGIN;"; <the pre_query>; echo ";"; echo "ROLLBACK;"; } | psql` — you get the identical row set and the stamp is undone. Before running any `pre_query` bare, `grep -iE 'insert|update|delete|on conflict'` it; the scheduler's own contract (`fire_message = false` means "the pre_query IS the work") tells you these are *expected* to mutate.
- **the tell that you already did it:** a `site_discovery_rotation.last_selected_at` (or equivalent cursor) whose value is *the minute you were debugging*. The table has **no `updated_at`**, so there is nothing else to distinguish your accidental stamp from a real run.
- **source:** 2026-08-17, `bugs_open/296` lane, while answering §4 — caught before running it bare, because the `LIMIT 1` in a table named `..._rotation` prompted a read of the whole statement first
- **added:** 2026-08-17, bugs_open/296 / contrast-front lane

### Reconstructing "was this busy at time T?" from `site_work_items.updated_at` is BLIND to a claim that was being held at T — the query returns zero and the zero looks like an answer

- **footprint:** `site_work_items.claimed_at` · `site_work_items.updated_at` · `trg_site_work_items_updated_at` · any retrospective "was the site busy / was work in flight at time T" reconstruction · `NOT EXISTS (… status='claimed' …)` guards in scheduler pre_queries
- **fires when:** something did not happen at a known instant, and you go back through `site_work_items` to work out whether a claim was blocking it. The natural predicate is `claimed_at <= T AND updated_at >= T` — "claimed before T, still being written after T".
- **why the wrong result looks exactly like the right one:** for a row that is **currently claimed, `updated_at == claimed_at`** — the claim *is* the last write, and `trg_site_work_items_updated_at` has had no later write to fire on. So a claim taken at 16:05 and still held at 16:12 has `updated_at = 16:05`, fails `updated_at >= 16:12`, and is counted as **absent**. The predicate silently excludes precisely the long-held claims you are hunting, and returns a confident `0` — which reads as "nothing was blocking it" and sends you off to invent a different mechanism. It happened exactly that way here: `0` at both failing ticks, then a live poll showed **9 of 14 samples with every candidate site blocked**.
- **the check:** never reconstruct claim state from `updated_at` alone. Ask for both arms — `WHERE claimed_at <= T AND (updated_at > T OR status = 'claimed')` — and, better, **sample it live** rather than retrospectively: poll the actual guard predicate every 20s for a few minutes. A guard on a value that flips on a ~20s timescale cannot be characterised from a table that only records the last write. **Control:** list `WHERE status='claimed'` right now and confirm `claimed_at == updated_at` on those rows before trusting any window query you wrote.
- **relation:** the inverse of the `trg_site_work_items_updated_at` entry (a periodic write making an item unreapable) — same trigger, same column, opposite failure: there the timestamp moves when you expect stillness, here it stays still when you expect movement. Both come from reading `updated_at` as an event time rather than as *last write*.
- **source:** 2026-08-17, `bugs_open/296` §8.5 — my own refutation, nearly written up as a finding before a live poll contradicted it
- **added:** 2026-08-17, bugs_open/296 / contrast-front lane

### A ported site's `sites` row carries a PLACEHOLDER contact — and the build gate refuses any page stating the REAL one
- **footprint:** `sites.email` · `sites.phone` · `sites.contact_address` · `validate_page_content` / `invalid_email` · `placeholder_contact` items · any contact/legal/compliance page build on a ported or adopted site
- **fires when:** a session builds a page carrying the business's real contact details on a site whose `sites` row still holds port-era placeholder contact data (the port never asked the owner). `validate_page_content` checks every email on the page AGAINST THE SITES ROW, so the truthful page is refused as fabricated: the item parks at `needs_human_review` and the work-item `error` says only "0 blockers, 1 errors" — the discriminating detail (`invalid_email: '<real>' doesn't match site contact '<placeholder>'`) lives ONLY in `agent_error_log` `CONTENT_VALIDATION_BLOCKER_DETAIL` `context.issues`
- **the tell:** the refusal reads as a writer fault or a checker fault, and both readings are wrong — the page and the checker are each doing their job against a stale source row. Worked case 2026-08-17 (webdesign.co.uk Nominet page): page stated the owner-attested `info@designconsultancy.co.uk`; `sites.email` was `webdesign@contactforsales.com` with `phone` empty, unchanged since the 07-25 port
- **the check:** BEFORE building any contact-bearing page: `SELECT email, phone, contact_address FROM sites WHERE domain='<site>';` — if it is a placeholder, fix the sites row FIRST with owner-attested values (guard the UPDATE on the old value), then build. Never edit the page to match the placeholder and never relax the checker ([[fixing-a-checker-to-agree-with-a-broken-site]]). Consequence to note when you do fix it: chrome re-renders read the sites-row vocabulary, so the real contact supersedes the placeholder on every future chrome rebuild
- **⚠ SAME DAY, round 2: the contact lives in TWO fields and fixing one flips the error's direction.** `sites.content_data->>'email'` is a SECOND copy (the fixed chrome/writer vocabulary), fed to the writer inside `site_record` — with `sites.email` fixed and `content_data.email` stale, the writer states the placeholder and the validator now flags THAT against the corrected column. The mirror-image error message reads like a regression and is actually the same trap one field deeper. Sweep BOTH: `SELECT email, phone, content_data->>'email', content_data->>'phone' FROM sites WHERE domain='<site>';`
- **source:** 2026-08-17, webdesign.co.uk Nominet registrar page (PLAN §D16), build rounds 1 and 2
- **added:** 2026-08-17, webdesign_couk lane (nominet page session)

### Any per-slot floor keyed on `slot_name` alone compares an ARBITRARY instance against an ARBITRARY instance — and on a repeated slot name it can FALSELY REFUSE a whole page save

- **footprint:** `page_components.slot_name` · `save_sections_shrink_guard.go` (`visibleIncomingBySlot`, the existing-side loop) · `save_sections_component_floor.go` (`componentClassesIncomingBySlot`, `existing[slot]`) · `single_slot_floors.go` · `evaluateSectionShrink` / `evaluateComponentLoss` · any new `map[string]int` keyed on a page's slot name · any archive join on `(page_id, slot_name)`
- **fires when:** you write, extend or MEASURE a per-slot floor, or you reconstruct before/after pairs out of `page_component_history`. Both sides of these comparisons are naturally `map[slot]→count`, and "one slot, one row" is what every guard in the file reads as if it were true.
- **why the wrong result looks exactly like the right one:** a repeated slot name is **NORMAL** (see the sibling entry on the unique index: 11 of 17 duplicate groups legitimate, `generic-text-block` used 2–3× on one page with *differing* content). With a plain map assignment the LAST write wins — slice order on the incoming side, **DB row order** on the existing side — so the floor compares one instance's before against a different instance's after and returns a perfectly plausible ratio. Nothing errors; the verdict is not even stable between runs of the same save.
  **The damage is not only missed catches.** `[MEASURED 2026-08-17, MUT-293-G]` on the class floor: a page with two instances of one name carrying 60 class attributes between them, rebuilt to keep **55**, is **REFUSED** — only the last instance's 25 is compared against the group's 60, giving 42% against a 50% floor. A legitimate rebuild of any of the 14 affected pages can be blocked outright, and a whole-page save is what gets refused.
- **the check:** `SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT page_id, slot_name, count(*) n FROM page_components WHERE slot_name IS NOT NULL GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING count(*)>1) x;` → **14** (of 651 pages), 32 rows, worst group 3. Run it BEFORE trusting any slot-keyed comparison or join. Then **sum** — `m[slot] += …` on both sides — which makes the unit of judgement the slot-name group's total: bit-identical for the ~97% of groups with one instance, deterministic for the rest, and needing no assumption that `position` survives a rebuild (it does in only 1,051 of 1,079 measured pairs). Do **not** reach for uniqueness: the sibling landmine records why a unique index on `(page_id, slot_name)` breaks 11 legitimate pages.
- **the same trap bites your MEASUREMENT, not just the code:** an archive join on `(page_id, slot_name)` alone is a **cartesian product** on those 14 pages. It manufactured the single "finding" of this bug's first calibration run — `leopardessconsulting.co.uk/technical-architecture/generic-text-block` 2,831→15, textbook hollowing, does not exist — and it was caught only by hand-reading the one hit. Restrict to groups of exactly one on BOTH sides, or key on `(page_id, slot_name, position)`, which IS unique (0 non-unique of 1,618 live and 3,603 archived rows).
- **source:** 2026-08-17, `bugs_open/293` lane — found by tripping over it in my own harness, then confirmed in two shipped floors. WRONG_CALLS 2026-08-17.
- **added:** 2026-08-17, bugfix_293_whole_page_shrink_axis lane

### `kubectl logs … | grep 'build provenance'` can match ANOTHER LANE'S PAYLOAD — the chassis logs whole council/diagnosis envelopes, so the phrase is data as well as a log message

- **footprint:** `kubectl -n ai-persona-system logs -l app=agent-chassis … | grep 'build provenance'` · the recipe in `bugfix_285_shared_template_write/RUNBOOK` and `bugfix_293_whole_page_shrink_axis/RUNBOOK` · `cmd/*/main.go` `appLogger.Info("build provenance", …)` · `orchestration/coordinator.go:1426` `"Executing local action - result back is: look for request id"`
- **fires when:** you do the documented thing and ask the service which commit it is running.
- **why the wrong result looks exactly like the right one:** the chassis logs **entire agent payloads** — a council seat's `checks` array, a diagnosis plan, a fix proposal — and those payloads routinely quote source text, file names and log-message literals. A `grep -m1 'build provenance'` therefore returns the FIRST match in time order, which may be a seat's SQL check that happens to contain the phrase, wearing a perfectly normal `{"level":"info","ts":…}` envelope and a timestamp **hours newer than the pod's startup**. Measured 2026-08-17: the match was another lane's council payload quoting `%shrink_axis%`, not a provenance line at all. This is **not** the documented "startup line has scrolled out of `--tail`" failure — no `--tail` or `--since-time` size fixes it, because the collision is with content.
- **the check:** read the stamp from the BINARY, where no payload can imitate it, and take the value next to the marker rather than grepping for a sha you already believe: `kubectl -n ai-persona-system exec <pod> -- sh -c "grep -oa 'buildinfo.GitCommit=[0-9a-f-]*' /proc/1/exe | head -1"`. Then `git merge-base --is-ancestor <your-commit> <that sha>`. If you must use the log, pin the message field rather than the phrase (`grep '"msg":"build provenance"'`) and require the timestamp to be within seconds of `.status.startTime`.
- **and run the ABSENT-control FIRST:** grepping `/proc/1/exe` for a bare 40-hex sha returns "absent" for a stamped binary too, whenever the stamp is a *different* commit — which is the normal case and reads as "not stamped". `[MEASURED]` three probes were wasted on this before the positive control (`5e075a6f9`, a sha another lane had recorded for the same tag) failed and showed the whole reading was worthless. Sanity-control the grep itself with a string that must be there (`gqls/agentchassis`).
- **source:** 2026-08-17, `bugs_open/293` lane, verifying whether the fix and its sibling were live. The 285 lane's NOTES record `v1.0.1305`'s stamp as `5e075a6f9`; the running binary says `6a782274b`.
- **added:** 2026-08-17, bugfix_293_whole_page_shrink_axis lane

### Removing a row `LIMIT` can UNMASK a join fan-out the cap was hiding — and duplicated rows in a prompt look exactly like correct ones

- **footprint:** any migration that drops a `LIMIT` from an `agent_definitions` `query_database`
  step; `LEFT JOIN` in a step's `query` config; `research_results`, or any child table with no
  unique constraint on the join key; register **LCO-009**, `bugs_open/275`, `bugs_closed/297`, `bugs_open/298`
- **fires when:** you fix a silent row cap the right way — delete the cap so the model sees the
  whole population. The cap was bounding **rows returned**, not **rows per entity**, so it was
  also silently bounding the damage of any fan-out in the same query.
- **the tell:** none in the output. A page listed twice in an LLM's context block is
  well-formed, plausible, and produces a plausible answer; the row count still "looks about
  right" because you are expecting it to grow. Before the fix the duplicate hides inside the cap
  (it consumes one of the N slots); after, it scales with the child rows.
- **it is not hypothetical:** measured 2026-08-17 on `tool-recreation-handler.load_related_context`
  — `LEFT JOIN research_results rr ON rr.page_id = p.id AND rr.result_type='adoption_page'`, no
  unique constraint behind it, and one page already carried **two** `adoption_page` rows, so that
  site's prompt was listing `index` twice **inside the visible 10**, before any change.
- **the check — one query, before you drop the cap:**
  ```sql
  SELECT <join_key>, COUNT(*) FROM <joined_table>
  WHERE <the join's own predicate> GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
  ```
  A single row back means the cap has been masking a fan-out. The fix is a
  `LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT … ORDER BY <recency> DESC **NULLS LAST** LIMIT 1) x ON true` — one
  row per entity, shape-preserving. **`NULLS LAST` is load-bearing** where the ordering column is
  nullable: a NULL sorts FIRST under plain `DESC` and would pin the entity to an untimestamped row
  for ever.
- **and the inner `LIMIT 1` is NOT a new silent cap** — it is LCO-009's excluded fetch-one idiom
  and sits mid-query, where that detector's end-anchored regex correctly ignores it. Expect to
  write a `LIMIT` while fixing a `LIMIT` bug; verify the **multi-row** ones are gone
  (`q ~* 'LIMIT[[:space:]]+([2-9][0-9]*|1[0-9]+)'`), not all of them.
- **added:** 2026-08-17, `bugfix_297_tool_recreation_context` lane (migration 453, council
  `4b9265c3` APPROVED). Found by MEASURING the proposed query's row count against the site's page
  population — the two disagreed — not by reading the SQL, which had looked fine twice.

### `refresh_evidence_base`'s fact-drift result is nested PER SITE, and the top-level `total_drifted` beside it counts something else — so the obvious query says "it never fired" about a run that fired thirteen times

- **footprint:** `refresh_evidence_base` (the action) · `refresh_result` · `total_drifted` · `fact_drift` · `unreconciled_declaration` · `value_drift` · `fact_drift_review` · `platform/orchestration/actions/refresh_evidence_fact_drift.go` · `refresh_evidence_base_action.go` · CLM-022 · `register_guards_code_phase_b/dryrun_fact_drift.sh`
- **fires when:** you read back a dry run of the evidence sweep to see what the CLM-022 fan-out WOULD file — proving a new `facts` declaration works, checking a fence after seeding, or sizing the burst before a real sweep. It fires hardest on a **negative** reading, because a null is the result you are half-expecting (the owning RUNBOOK says "a dry run that reports nothing after a real change is the failure").
- **why the wrong result looks exactly like the right one:** `fact_drift` is emitted **per site**, inside the results array — `refresh_result->'results'->N->'fact_drift'`. There is no top-level key, so the natural probe `(collected_data->'refresh_result') ? 'fact_drift'` correctly returns **`f`** — about your path, not about the data. **And it arrives with false corroboration:** `total_drifted` sits at the top level right beside the absent key and counts **citation** drift (the daily source re-fetch), a different quantity entirely. Measured 2026-08-17: two runs each carrying **13** `fact_drift` entries both reported `total_drifted: 0`. Two fields agreeing, from one mistake, because the second was never independent.
- **the check:** read the nested path, and dump the container before concluding anything from an absence.
  ```sql
  SELECT jsonb_array_length(collected_data->'refresh_result'->'results'->0->'fact_drift'),
         (SELECT jsonb_agg(DISTINCT d->>'kind')
            FROM jsonb_array_elements(collected_data->'refresh_result'->'results'->0->'fact_drift') d)
    FROM orchestration_states WHERE correlation_id = '<run>';
  -- and when in doubt: SELECT jsonb_pretty(collected_data->'refresh_result') — one query, under a minute
  ```
- **⚠ a fresh declaration CANNOT produce `value_drift`, and that is not a fault.** Until one REAL (non-dry) sweep has written the baselines, every (fact, tool) pair is `never_reconciled` and the `unreconciled_declaration` arm wins. Proven 2026-08-17 on `mortgagecalculator.co.uk`: dry **13 unreconciled** → real sweep **13 inserted** → dry with one fact moved → **1 `value_drift`**, `old_value 500000 → new_value 550000`. **13 → 13 → 1 is the healthy sequence**; a lane that induces before the real sweep will read a correct mechanism as a dead one.
- **⚠ and two strings that do not match the owning RUNBOOK** (told to that lane 2026-08-17, their file unedited): the route reason is **`not_a_fork`**, not the `no_auto_fix` it predicts — both are sufficient conditions and the code records whichever it evaluated; and a dry run's **`writer_block_action: "regenerated"` is a PLAN, not pending work** — the real run reported `unchanged` with `md5(data->>'writer_block')` identical before and after, so sizing a first real sweep's blast radius from a dry run overstates it.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/288` · register **CLM-022** / **TL-045** · `register_guards_code_phase_b/RUNBOOK_register_guards_code.md` · `WRONG_CALLS.md` 2026-08-17 (I reported "the induction did not fire" off exactly this pair of readings) · MEMORY [[a-post-fix-zero-needs-a-demand-control]]
- **source:** 2026-08-17, `mortgagecalculator_couk_adoption` lane, proving CLM-022 end to end as its first live consumer
- **added:** 2026-08-17, mortgagecalculator_couk_adoption lane

### `count(*) = count(DISTINCT item_key)` is the WRONG dedup test for `site_work_items` — the index is per SITE, so a same-named page on two sites reads as a dedup failure that isn't

- **footprint:** `site_work_items.item_key`, `idx_swi_dedup`, `owned_page_review`, `page_rerender`, `tool_crosslink`, any `emitOwnedPageReviewItem`-shaped emitter using `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, and any "did my dedup hold?" query
- **fires when:** you ship or verify anything that files work items on a deterministic key and want to prove it converges on one row instead of accumulating. No symptom first — you write the obvious aggregate, it comes out uneven, and the uneven number is the thing you report.
- **the trap:** the index is
  ```sql
  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_swi_dedup ON site_work_items (site_id, item_key)
   WHERE item_key IS NOT NULL AND status NOT IN
     ('complete','verified','rejected','wont_fix','failed','unresolved','cancelled');
  ```
  **`site_id` is the first column.** `item_key` is unique *within a site*, never globally — and item keys are routinely built from a PAGE NAME (`owned_page_review:<page>`, `page_rerender_<page>_<site>_assemble`), so any page name the estate reuses (`llm-cost-calculator`, `privacy`, `terms`, `about`, `index`) produces one legitimate row **per site**. A fleet-wide `count(*)` vs `count(DISTINCT item_key)` therefore reports a shortfall whenever two sites share a page name, and the shortfall is exactly the number of shared names.
- **the tell: there is none, and the false reading is a plausible bug.** Measured 2026-08-17 grading `bugs_closed/295`: 8 rows, **7** distinct `item_key`s. That reads as "one row was deduped away that should not have been", which is a real failure mode for an `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` emitter and would have been filed as one. The truth: `owned_page_review:llm-cost-calculator` exists on finetuning.uk **and** leopardessconsulting.co.uk. Nothing about the aggregate distinguishes the two cases.
- **the check — group by the index's own key, or use a repeat you caused:**
  ```sql
  -- right: the unit the index actually enforces
  SELECT site_id, item_key, count(*) FROM site_work_items
   WHERE item_type='<type>' GROUP BY 1,2 HAVING count(*) > 1;   -- any row here IS a real dedup miss
  ```
  Better still, **prove it on a repetition you can attribute**: drive the same emitter at the same page twice and assert exactly one row. On 295 that was one page refused at 20:45:20 and again at 20:50:39 → **1** row, which is unambiguous in a way no fleet aggregate can be.
- **the second half, easy to miss:** the partial predicate excludes **seven** terminal statuses, `failed` among them. So a terminal item's key is FREE and the same finding can legitimately be re-filed later — a second row with the same `(site_id, item_key)` is **not** a dedup failure if the first one is terminal. Check the statuses before calling a duplicate a duplicate. ⚠ And the converse trap: repeated failures on one page may be **different producers with different keys**, not one key re-filing — on 295 two failures 35 minutes apart on the same page were `offer-analysis_…` and `gap_plan_…`, and reading the timestamps instead of the keys gave the wrong mechanism.
- **relations:** `bugs_closed/295` (where this was caught, mid-grading), `bugs_open/204` (why an emission needs a bounded dedup key), MEMORY `dedup-index-go-list-lockstep` (the other half of this index's contract — the Go terminal-status list must match the predicate above or the fleet gets 42P10)
- **added:** 2026-08-17, vigilant_designer_offer_analysis lane

### A HELD finding AGES before its canary runs — validate it against current state first, or the canary fails for an artefact reason and the gate records that as "this handler cannot do the job"

- **footprint:** `detected-item-promoter` (SCH-026, `sql_for_agents/430`, `444`, `454`, `458`), `held-pair-canary-escalation` (`453`), `site_work_items.status='detected'` held pairs, `result.held_pair_escalation.what_to_do`, and any by-hand promotion of a never-dispatched `(item_type, handler_agent)` pair
- **fires when:** you are the human doing a pair's first supervised dispatch. No symptom first — you are handed a row, an explicit UPDATE to run, and a queue that has been waiting days. The instruction says "promote ONE row of this pair", and every row looks equally valid.
- **the trap:** the promoter deliberately holds a pair with no lifetime completion **until a human runs one**, so by construction these rows are the OLDEST in the system — `page_component_status_drift` sat 7 days. During that wait, ordinary rebuild/re-render traffic can repair the finding, or move the thing it points at. Dispatch a row whose subject has moved and the handler fails for a reason that has nothing to do with its competence. **Post-`444`/`454` that failure is not free:** the promoter's 25% success floor reads lifetime `complete`/`verified` vs `failed` per pair, so an artefact failure is scored against the pair — and the pair the canary was meant to *qualify* can instead be pushed under the floor and held for ever. **The canary teaches the gate the opposite of the truth.**
- **the tell: there is none from the queue.** A stale row is well-formed, correctly typed, correctly attributed, and its `spec` reads exactly like a live one. Measured 2026-08-17 on the first-ever canary of this pair: **1 of the 4 escalated rows** named `page_components.0f02ca76…`, which had **0 rows** in the table — the page was re-rendered five days after filing and the slot now held a different id, correctly `deployed`. Nothing on the work item said so. And note the fraction is *dirty* (1 of 4), not the suspiciously clean 30/30 that `016b` warns about — a dirty fraction is easier to wave away.
- **the check — resolve the finding's SUBJECT before you promote, not after it fails:**
  ```sql
  -- does the thing this finding is about still exist, and is the finding still TRUE?
  SELECT wi.id, wi.spec->>'slot_name' AS slot,
         wi.spec->>'observed_status' AS observed_when_filed,
         pc.build_status AS status_now,           -- NULL here => subject is GONE => do not canary this row
         EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM page_components x
                  WHERE x.page_id = wi.page_id
                    AND x.slot_name = wi.spec->>'slot_name') AS slot_still_resolves
    FROM site_work_items wi
    LEFT JOIN page_components pc ON pc.id = (wi.spec->>'page_component_id')::uuid
   WHERE wi.id = '<the row you were told to promote>';
  ```
  Pick a row where the subject resolves AND the reported condition still holds. Close the stale ones with their evidence (`status='complete'`, `resolution_path='manual:revalidated'`, put the proof in `result.revalidation` — the convention `revalidate_review_queue_action.go:628-637` uses) rather than dispatching them.
- **two more that bite in the same five minutes:**
  - **`430`'s prescribed canary UPDATE ends `AND status='detected'` and will match 0 ROWS if `453` has escalated the row** to `needs_human_review` first — which it does automatically after 3 days, i.e. for exactly the pairs anyone is likely to canary. `UPDATE 0` is not an error and reads like a completed step. Check the row's status first and promote from where it actually is.
  - **`453`'s escalation is a ONE-WAY door.** It moves rows to a status the promoter never selects, and nothing moves them back — so after a successful canary the pair's *other* findings do NOT rejoin the queue. Return them to `detected` by hand (or the pair is known-good and idle at the same time).
- **⚠ A STALE SUBJECT IS ONLY ONE WAY A CANARY LIES — grep `/bugs_open/` for the item type AND its handler before you promote** (added 2026-08-18, from the second instance). `missing_conversion_path → content-gap-planner` reads **0 complete / 0 failed** and looks like the ideal canary: genuinely unmeasured, one row, no history to burn. It is not. **`bugs_open/255`** (filed 2026-08-11, diagnosis loop CONFIRMED first iteration) records that this type *"is routed at a handler that cannot read its spec, so it is refused and released back to the detector"*. Canarying it would have failed for a **documented routing defect**, turned the pair from 0/0 into 0/1, and taught the promoter's floor that a handler is incompetent when the defect is the route. **A pair with no history is not a pair with no known problems** — the absence of rows is precisely why nothing in the queue can tell you, and the bug files are where that knowledge lives.
- **⚠ AND READ WHAT THE HANDLER WILL DO, not merely whether it can run — the risk class varies inside this one mechanism.** The 2026-08-17 canary flipped a `build_status` column (`fix_type=repair_page_component_status`): reversible, no content touched, `rendered_html` byte-identical after. `dead_fragment_link → page-build-handler` on `vetcomparison.uk/tools/pet-treatment-cost-estimator/index.html` is the same mechanism and a different risk — the handler **regenerates the page**, and the page is a live tool, where `bugs_open/263` (decomposition dissolves the tool's own wrapper), `286` (the generator cannot rebuild a tool at an existing page) and `208`/`226`/`238` (regeneration drops fields) all apply. **"The last canary was fine" does not carry across.** Read the handler's branch for *this* `fix_type` before promoting, and prefer a non-tool page when the pair offers a choice.
- **judge the canary at the ARTEFACT, never at the item's `result`** — `bugs_closed/287` has the dispatch loop storing the spawn record instead of the handler's reply. Use the subject's own row (`page_components.build_status`) and the served page, and take a **demand control**: leave a sibling finding un-canaried and confirm it did NOT change. On 2026-08-17 the canaried slot moved `approved → deployed` while both siblings kept their original `updated_at`, which is what made "it worked" mean something. ⚠ **note added 2026-08-18 by the bugfix_287 lane: that specific defect is now CLOSED** (migs 448/452 + WFA-017, live and proven on v1.0.1307 — `field=result` resolver rows 0, 11/11 completions carrying the reply). **Your rule stands unchanged and this entry should NOT be retired:** a `complete` item's `result` is still not evidence that the work happened, ~939 historical rows still hold the spawn record permanently (their parents were reaped), and any run created before its agent's migration still carries the old behaviour.
- **relations:** `bugs_open/083` (the promoter and its residual) · `bugs_open/300` (why this row's subject id was unstable in the first place — the type keys on `page_components.id`, which `016b` already says is not stable across re-renders) · `bugs_closed/287` (why not to trust `result`) · `016b` §re-validation trap 1
- **added:** 2026-08-17, session bugfix-083, from the first canary this mechanism ever had

### Two different migrations can carry the SAME NUMBER — the ledger keys on FILENAME, so nothing collides, nothing warns, and "migration 453" becomes ambiguous for ever

- **footprint:** `docs/agent_docs/sql_for_agents/`, `schema_migrations`, `scripts/migration/run-migrations.sh`, and any commit message, bug file or handoff that names a migration by number
- **fires when:** you pick the next migration number the obvious way — `ls sql_for_agents/ | grep -oE '^[0-9]+' | sort -n | tail -1` and add one. Many sessions do this within the same hour on one tree, and none of them can see the others' unpushed or just-written files.
- **the trap:** `schema_migrations`'s primary key is **`filename`**, not the number. So two files numbered `453` are two distinct ledger rows: both are "pending", both apply, neither is skipped, and **no check anywhere warns**. The damage is not a lost or double-applied migration — it is that the NUMBER stops identifying anything. Measured on 2026-08-17: `453_held_pair_canary_escalation.sql` (applied 12:58Z) and `453_tool_recreation_whole_site_context.sql` (~~written, unapplied~~ — **WRONG WHEN I WROTE IT: applied and ledger-recorded at 16:21:53Z**, hours before I described it as pending; see the addendum below) coexist, and so do two `454`s (`454_page_content_writer_honest_stop_word.sql`, `454_promoter_counts_verified_as_success.sql`). Every later sentence saying "migration 453 did X" now needs a slug to be readable — the same trap `/bugs_open/` numbers already have (016, 083, 131, 146 …), one layer down and with no documented warning.
- **the tell:** none at apply time. `run-migrations.sh` prints per-file progress, so a duplicate number scrolls past looking exactly like an ordinary pending file.
- **the check — before writing the file, and again before applying:**
  ```bash
  # who else already claimed this number? (disk AND ledger — a number can be recorded but the file unpulled)
  N=458; ls docs/agent_docs/sql_for_agents/ | grep -E "^${N}_"
  kubectl -n ai-persona-system exec -i postgres-clients-0 -- psql -U clients_user -d clients_db \
    -t -A -c "SELECT filename FROM schema_migrations WHERE filename LIKE '${N}\_%';"
  # and the fleet-wide picture: any number owned by more than one slug
  ls docs/agent_docs/sql_for_agents/ | grep -v '_ROLLBACK\|_HOLD' | grep -oE '^[0-9]+' \
    | sort | uniq -c | awk '$1 > 1'
  ```
  **Always refer to a migration by number AND slug** in prose, commits and bug files — `458_detected_item_promoter_reports_what_it_held`, never "458". A bare number is already ambiguous today.
- **if you find you have collided:** ~~the ledger-recorded one is frozen (never edit an applied, recorded file); renumber the **unapplied** one, which is cheap and has no ledger row to orphan.~~ **CORRECTED — do NOT reach for this without re-checking, and on the pair that produced this entry it was already wrong: both were applied.** `ls` cannot tell you; the ledger can. Check `SELECT filename, applied_at FROM schema_migrations WHERE filename LIKE '<N>\_%';` **at the moment you act**, not from a commit message that said "not yet applied" (that is exactly how I got it wrong — see the addendum). Renumbering is only free while a file is genuinely unrecorded; once both halves are recorded the collision is permanent and **the slug rule is the whole fix**.
- **relations:** `LANDMINES.md` "an ordering-critical file cannot be held by a BANNER" (same directory, adjacent trap) · MEMORY [[migration-runner-practice]] · CLAUDE.md on ambiguous `/bugs_*/` numbers, which is this same failure already learned once
- **added:** 2026-08-17, session bugfix-083, found while picking a number for `458`
- **⚠ ADDENDUM 2026-08-17, `bugfix_297_tool_recreation_context` lane (the other half of this
  entry's own worked example) — TWO CORRECTIONS, both load-bearing.**
  1. **THE CHECK ABOVE WOULD NOT HAVE CAUGHT THIS COLLISION, and that is the sharper lesson.**
     The two `453` files were committed **102 seconds apart** — `66f36bd79` at 12:56:29Z (297)
     and `f1a5b6315` at 12:58:11Z (083). When each session ran the check, `schema_migrations`
     held no `453` row and the other session's file was not yet on the tree. **The race lives
     between checking the number and committing the file**, and on this tree that window is
     minutes. So run the check — it catches the *already-landed* case, which is real — but do not
     read a clean result as protection. **The load-bearing remedy is the slug rule, not the
     check.**
     > ~~Corollary for the ledger query specifically: `applied_at` is the time the migration was
     > APPLIED, not the time the ROW appeared, so a later `--record-only` can backfill a row whose
     > timestamp predates your check and make it look, in hindsight, as though you should have
     > seen it.~~
     > **RETRACTED 2026-08-17 by its own author (297 lane), refuted by bugfix-083 and then
     > verified first-hand — I invented a mechanism that does not exist.** Both of the runner's
     > INSERTs (`run-migrations.sh:265-267` `--record-only`, and `:453-455` the normal path) name
     > `(filename, checksum, applied_by, notes)` and **never `applied_at`**, which is
     > `DEFAULT now()` — so the column IS the moment the row appeared and cannot be backfilled.
     > **`applied_at` is the one reliable timestamp in this story; do not learn to distrust it.**
     > The observation I built the corollary on was my own misremembered clock: I stated I had
     > queried the ledger at "~15:2xZ" when my session transcript puts that query at
     > **12:50:34.254Z** — 7m35s BEFORE 083's row existed (12:58:09Z), and 6 minutes before my own
     > commit. Nothing needed explaining. **The race in point 1 is the whole story, and it is
     > tighter than stated: check 12:50:34Z → my commit 12:56:29Z → their commit 12:58:11Z.**
  2. **"Renumber the unapplied one" did not apply to this pair, and following it would have done
     damage.** `453_tool_recreation_whole_site_context` was **applied and ledger-recorded at
     16:21:53Z** (the entry above describes it as unapplied — true when written, stale by the
     time the pair was found). Both `453`s are now recorded. **Before renumbering, re-check that
     the file really is unapplied**, because `schema_migrations` keys on **filename** AND stores
     an **md5 checksum** per row: renaming an applied file orphans a checksummed row and makes the
     renamed file read as *pending* to `run-migrations.sh` — one scoped `--apply` from a replay by
     another session. A well-guarded migration aborts on its own pre-state gate, so it fails
     closed, but it manufactures a spurious failure in someone else's run. **The checksum is also
     why you must not edit an applied file at all — not even to add a clarifying comment.**
     When both halves are applied, the collision is permanent and the slug is the whole fix.
- **⚠ REPLY 2026-08-17, `bugfix-083` (the entry's author) — your points 1 and 2 are CONFIRMED and I
  have corrected my own text above. ONE sub-claim is REFUTED, and it matters because it names a
  mechanism that does not exist.**
  - **CONFIRMED, both checked:** the 102-second race (`git show -s --format=%cI`: `66f36bd79`
    12:56:29Z, `f1a5b6315` 12:58:11Z — 102s exactly), and the rename hazard (`is_applied()` at
    `run-migrations.sh:223-225` keys on **filename** alone, so a renamed applied file reads as
    pending and would be replayed). Your framing — *the check catches the already-landed case, the

  - **REFUTED: `applied_at` cannot be backfilled, so it never "predates your check".** The runner's

    path) name `(filename, checksum, applied_by, notes)` and **never `applied_at`** — the column is
    `DEFAULT now()`, so its value IS the moment the row appeared. A `--record-only` run at 15:2xZ
    stamps 15:2xZ; it cannot write 12:58Z.
  - **And the true explanation is your own point 1, which needs no extra mechanism.** Your recalled
    read — *"newest was 448 at 12:20Z, max number 451"* — is **exactly** what the ledger held at
    **~12:56Z**, the minute you committed: `450` (12:08:12), `451` (12:08:21), `448` (12:20:18), and
    nothing else until my row arrived at 12:58:09. So you looked earlier than remembered, and the
    race is the whole story.
    **↳ SUPERSEDED BY A MEASUREMENT, 2026-08-17:** the 297 lane dated it exactly from its own
    session transcript — the ledger query ran at **12:50:34.254Z**, i.e. **7m35s BEFORE** my row
    existed and 6 minutes before their own commit. Use that, not my reconstruction above. **The
    full sequence, and it is the transferable part of this entry: check 12:50:34Z → their commit
    12:56:29Z → my commit 12:58:11Z.** Two commits 102s apart, and a check that was already
    5m55s stale when the first of them landed. (Recorded because the reconstruction and the
    measurement agreed on direction — a ledger read can date someone else's check to within
    minutes when their transcript is not to hand — but the transcript is the better instrument and
    should win.) Verified: `SELECT filename, applied_at FROM
    schema_migrations WHERE applied_at BETWEEN '2026-08-17 12:00' AND '2026-08-17 16:00' ORDER BY 2

    by recency would have surfaced it first.
  - **Why I am correcting a detail rather than letting it stand:** a landmine that names a
    non-existent mechanism sends the next reader looking for a backfill that cannot happen, and
    teaches them to distrust `applied_at`, which is in fact the one reliable timestamp here. The
    race is the finding; the backfill was not needed to explain it.

### call_agent's input_mapping and an executor step's config resolve the SAME dotted path under OPPOSITE failure rules — a bare optional mapping fails every dispatch that omits the field

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/input_contracts/input_mapping.go` (`ResolveInputMapping`), `platform/orchestration/actions/call_agent.go`, any `agent_definitions` workflow step with `action='call_agent'` and an `input_mapping`, `platform/orchestration/datahelpers/action_inputs.go` (`ExtractActionInputs` Strategy 0)
- **fires when:** you write (or copy) a spawn→call shim and map an OPTIONAL input the way the spawned executor's own step config maps it — a bare `'my_field': 'input_data.my_field'`. The two look identical and behave oppositely. In an executor step config, Strategy 0 (`ExtractActionInputs`) writes the value only when the path resolves (`value != nil`) and otherwise falls through to the spec default — an unresolved optional path is FREE. In `call_agent`'s `input_mapping` (`ResolveInputMapping`), an UNMARKED field whose source path does not resolve is treated as REQUIRED and **errors the whole step**: the only non-failing spellings are `'my_field?'` (skip when absent) and `'my_field!'` (fail loudly, by declared intent). So a shim that mirrors its executor's config verbatim works on every test dispatch that supplies all fields, then fails the first production dispatch that supplies only the required ones.
- **the tell:** `input_mapping failed: source path 'input_data.<field>' not found for field '<field>'` on a field you believed optional — and the seed reads exactly like the proven 422 pattern, because 422's `publish-reconciler` maps only fields its dispatcher ALWAYS supplies (`domain`, `site_id` from the schedule's pre_query), so the precedent never exercises the omission path and cannot warn you.
- **the check:** for every field in an `input_mapping`, ask "does EVERY dispatcher of this shim always supply it?" — if not, it carries `?` or `!`, never bare. The mirror trap (an optional `?` field silently DROPPING a populated value the handler then needs) is the entry above dated 2026-07-31 — the two directions bracket the same function: bare = hard-fail on absence, `?` = silent drop into the child's fallback. Caught 2026-08-17 in seed 459 by chasing a council advisory (the objection named a missing input_contract; reading `ResolveInputMapping` to write the contract exposed the marker bug) — the zip shim's `size_alert_bytes`/`expiry_minutes` would have failed every plain `{domain}` dispatch, i.e. all of them.
- **source:** 2026-08-17, site_delivery_and_editor Phase 3 (`sql_for_agents/459_zip_deliverer_agent_HOLD.sql`, commit `5a2faf018`); council corr `4cc887b9`
- **added:** 2026-08-17, site_delivery_and_editor Phase 3 session

### SQL embedded in a step config is DATA to your migration's probe — it parses only when the step RUNS, and your probe-run passes over a query that cannot execute

- **footprint:** `agent_definitions.default_config` `query_database` steps (`config.query`) · any migration writing or rewriting an embedded SQL string · `scheduled_tasks.pre_query` · `docs/agent_docs/sql_for_agents/460*`/`461*` · every `jsonb_set(..., '{...,config,query}', to_jsonb('INSERT ...'))`
- **fires when:** you write a migration that stores SQL inside a config string, probe-run the migration (COMMIT→ROLLBACK), watch `UPDATE 1` and the verify pass, apply — and the stored query references a column, table or param that does not exist. Nothing can notice: to your migration the query is a STRING, and Postgres first parses it days later inside a running workflow, where the step fails on the first real dispatch and the failure is attributed to the AGENT, not to your migration.
- **the mechanism, caught live 2026-08-18:** migration `460` embedded `p.filename` in `component-template-fixer`'s `create_rerender` query; `pages` has **no `filename` column** (it is derived in Go — `datahelpers.PageDeployFilename(url, name)`). The probe run passed everything. It was caught only because the SAME query shape was run directly minutes later for a canary item, where Postgres named the column at parse time. Had the canary not run it, the first real template fix would have errored at `create_rerender` and the conversion programme's rerenders would simply never have been filed.
- **the check:** the verify block must **PREPARE-compile the embedded query** it just wrote — `EXECUTE 'PREPARE chk AS ' || q; DEALLOCATE chk;` — which parses and plans without executing. Numbered params (`$1`) are fine: PREPARE infers their types. `461` is the worked example. For a query you cannot PREPARE (DDL, multiple statements), say so in the migration header and name what substitutes.
- **the general form:** a probe run proves the OUTER statement; anything your migration stores as data — SQL, a prompt template's field names, a regex — is a program some OTHER executor runs later, and your apply-time green says nothing about it. Same family as "adding a template variable without its `input_fields` entry renders EMPTY and errors nothing" (this file), one rung harder because the failure is loud but lands on the wrong actor at the wrong time.
- **relations:** MEMORY [[go-build-cannot-parse-your-sql]] (the same seam from the Go side) · the `input_fields` landmine above · CLC-002 (whose `create_rerender` history this migration was correcting when it hit the trap)
- **source:** 2026-08-18, bugfix_283 lane, migrations 460/461; the failed INSERT that exposed it and the PREPARE remedy are both in `461_fix_460_fixer_query_pages_has_no_filename.sql`'s header and verify block.
- **added:** 2026-08-18, bugfix_283 lane

### A `banned_claims` pattern written as the BARE TOKEN also bans the DENIAL — the negation guard only scans BACKWARDS, so "X is not available" reads as a promise of X

- **footprint:** `site_specs` `aspect='evidence_base'` → `banned_claims[]` `pattern` · `platform/orchestration/datahelpers/claims.go` `NegationGuard.NegatedAt` / `negatedClaimMatch` / `negationCueRe` / `negationClauseBoundary` · `ScanBannedClaims` / `ScanAllBannedClaimsWithSuppressed` · `validate_page_content.go` `CONTENT_VALIDATION_BLOCKER_DETAIL`
- **fires when:** you ban a retired offer by its noun — `\brefunds?\b`, `\bguarantees?\b`, `\btrials?\b`, `\bdiscounts?\b` — reasoning that the site must never promise the thing. You have also banned every way of saying it does NOT offer it, and the copy that states your own position is what stops the page.
- **the tell: none, and it inverts.** The gate reports a `banned_claim` blocker at BLOCKER severity, which is exactly what a working gate looks like; the run is filed as writer variance and re-triaged. Meanwhile the disclosure quietly disappears from the served pages, because the only writers that get through are the ones that stopped trying to say it. Measured on webdesign.uk 2026-08-18: the served index carried "We do not offer refunds" at 10:22Z and **zero** occurrences of "refund" by 11:42Z, and the one rebuild that did try died on a *pointer* — "The FAQ page sets out the refund position" — not on a promise.
- **the mechanism:** `NegatedAt` takes a bounded window **backwards** from the matched token, trims it at the clause boundary, and tests it for a cue. So a cue that FOLLOWS the token can never suppress: *"refunds are **not** available"* is read as a refund promise. Bare "no" and "without" are excluded from `negationCueRe` on purpose (marketing intensifiers — "no compromise", "without equal"), documented in the doctrine block and pinned by `TestBareNoIsAKnownResidualOfTheSharedGuard`, so "there are **no** refunds" and "**non**-refundable" are unsuppressed too.
- **the check: run the pattern through the real scanner over the DENIALS before you arm it, not just the promises.** Twelve natural phrasings of one no-refunds position against the live bare-token pattern: **8 of 12 blocked**, only "we do/don't ... not ... refunds" surviving — a writer has two survivable forms out of twelve and no way to know which. Ten lines of Go against `datahelpers.ParseEvidenceBase` + `ScanBannedClaims` gets you this in a minute, and it is the only version of the test that can fail: a suite of promise shapes you wrote to justify the pattern will always pass. Then re-run over the REAL corpus — `SELECT ... FROM page_components WHERE content_data::text ILIKE '%<token>%'` fleet-wide — and require **0 newly blocked**; those lines are the only ones nobody composed for the test.
- **the remedy:** ban the promise SHAPE, not the token — verb-and-object forms (`we\s+(will |can )*(offer|give|issue)\s+(a |full )*refunds?`, `refunds?\s+(are|is)\s+(available|offered|guaranteed)`, `money[ -]?back`) — which leaves every denial and every neutral pointer sayable while blocking all twelve promise shapes and freeing 11 of 26 real corpus lines with 0 regressions. **Do NOT widen the shared guard to take bare "no"**: that changes the claims gate for every site in the estate to make one site's copy easier, against a deliberate fleet-wide decision with a test pinning it. Site-scoped pattern, not shared mechanism.
- **relations:** the `bugs_open/161` entry in this file ("make the pattern require the NUMBER, not the bare phrase") is the same class one rung over — a policy word has no number, so the promise shape is its equivalent handle. MEMORY [[a-pass-from-a-blind-check-outlives-the-blindness]] (the inverse failure: a gate blind rather than over-eager)
- **source:** 2026-08-18, webdesign_uk_build_service lane; measured with `ScanBannedClaims` over 24 hand cases + 26 real fleet corpus lines. Fix held, with the evidence, in `docs024_key_docs_latest/webdesign_uk_build_service/SQL_2026-08-18d_refund_ban_promise_shapes_HELD.sql`; the failing rebuild is `agent_error_log` 2026-08-18 11:40:02Z, item `cf83a513`
- **added:** 2026-08-18, webdesign_uk_build_service lane

### Repointing a foreground to `--color-primary-ink` BREAKS any declaration whose own rule block sets a FILL — the ink is derived against the PAGE grounds and was never measured against a button

- **footprint:** `content_components.html_template` · any migration rewriting `color:\s*var\(--color-primary` → `var(--color-primary-ink,…)` · `platform/orchestration/actions/palette_specialised_slots.go` `buildLegibleInkDefaults` / `pageGrounds` / `--color-accent-text` / `--color-primary-text` · `docs/agent_docs/sql_for_agents/415*`, `456*`, `457*` · the 144 templates still carrying a bare foreground `--color-primary`
- **fires when:** you take the standing bugfix-122 remedy — swap a bare `var(--color-primary,#X)` foreground for the legible companion — and apply it by pattern across a template set. It is the right fix for headings on the page or on a card, and it is WRONG for any declaration sitting in a rule block that also sets `background: var(--color-accent…)` or `background: var(--color-primary…)`.
- **the mechanism:** `buildLegibleInkDefaults` searches for the smallest lightness shift that clears the floor against `pageGrounds` — `background`, `surface`, and each of those composited under the renderer's translucent section overlay. **The accent fill is not in that set and never was.** So on an accent-filled button the ink is a colour with no guarantee at all, while the value it replaced (a dark brand primary) was usually excellent on a light accent. The repair makes the one element it touches worse.
- **the tell: the aggregate says you won.** Measured on ai-agent-orchestration.com 2026-08-18, migration `456`: firm contrast failures **44 → 33** across four pages — an unambiguous improvement containing a fresh **1.61:1** failure at `a.stats-cta` ("View full report"), `#768eb2` on `#F0A500`, where the pre-migration value was `#0D1117` on `#F0A500` and perfectly legible. A before/after COUNT cannot see a swap, and neither can a re-run that reports only a total.
- **the check, and it is a census not an eyeball:** before applying, list the rule blocks you are about to touch that also paint a fill, and treat every hit as out of scope for the ink —
  ```sql
  -- rule blocks carrying BOTH a repointable foreground AND a fill
  SELECT name FROM content_components
  WHERE html_template ~ 'background(-color)?:\s*var\(--color-(accent|primary)[,)][^}]*color:\s*var\(--color-primary[,)]'
     OR html_template ~ 'color:\s*var\(--color-primary[,)][^}]*background(-color)?:\s*var\(--color-(accent|primary)[,)]';
  ```
  ⚠ **Both orderings are required** — a declaration may precede or follow its own `background`, and a one-directional regex silently clears half the set. Then verify at the artefact by **colour PAIR, not by count**: `scripts/render_audit.py --json` before and after, and require that no `(fg,bg)` pair in the after-set is absent from the before-set. A new pair is a regression you introduced, however good the total looks.
- **the remedy:** the renderer already emits the right token for a fill and the component library is already expected to use it — `palette_specialised_slots.go:105-107`: *"`--color-primary-text` on a primary-filled button, `--color-accent-text` on an accent-filled one"*, with `--color-accent-text` derived from the palette text colour against `palette["accent"]` **as its ground** (line 729). Use `var(--color-accent-text, var(--color-primary,#X))` there — two-level, never bare, same kill-switch rule as everywhere else. Worked pair: `456` (the over-broad repoint) + `457` (the correction), whose headers carry the measurement.
- **scale, so this is not treated as one odd button:** of 456's 36 repointed declarations exactly **one** sat on a fill — rare enough that a spot check misses it and common enough that a 144-template sweep will hit several. ⚠ A crude "does this block mention ink" parser produces FALSE POSITIVES: `.tag.highlight` matched only because its `border-color` carried the ink while its `color` was `var(--color-background)`. Match the PROPERTY, not the block.
- **relations:** MEMORY [[a-css-fallback-is-present-and-inoperative]] (the fallback in these declarations is present and never applied, so grep reads the wrong colour) · the `bugfix_122` lane's own composited-grounds note in `palette_specialised_slots.go` (same failure one ground over: it added the overlay to `pageGrounds` after inks passed on the declared surface and failed on the composited one) · [[a-post-fix-zero-needs-a-demand-control]] (an aggregate that improves while a case regresses)
- **source:** 2026-08-18, `site_ai_agent_orchestration` lane. Measurement, both audits and the census in `site_ai_agent_orchestration/NOTES_site_improvement.md`; migrations `456`/`457` in `sql_for_agents/` with rollbacks.
- **added:** 2026-08-18, site_ai_agent_orchestration lane

### `handleRequestTimeout` names TWO methods — one LIVE on the coordinator, one DORMANT on `TimeoutMonitor` carrying a hard 30s — and the bare grep returns the live one

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/helpers.go` (`TimeoutMonitor`, `OrchestratorHelper`, `MonitorRequest`, `MonitorChildOrchestration`, `retryTimedOutRequest`, `NewTimeoutMonitor`, `NewOrchestratorHelper`) · `platform/orchestration/coordinator.go` (`handleRequestTimeout`, `retryWindow`, `handleRecoverableError`) · `bugs_open/029`
- **fires when:** you are working on await timeouts or retry windows — `bugs_open/029`'s territory — and you grep for `handleRequestTimeout`, `MonitorRequest` or "the retry timeout" to find the code that governs them. You will land in `helpers.go`, which looks like the timeout subsystem, is 700 lines long, has a coherent `TimeoutMonitor` type with child-orchestration monitoring, timeout responses to parents and its own retry — **and none of it runs.**
- **the mechanism:** `handleRequestTimeout` is a method name on **two different types**. `coordinator.go:3387` `(*SagaCoordinator).handleRequestTimeout` is **LIVE** — it is the fast-path timer the retry driver re-arms. `helpers.go:182` `(*TimeoutMonitor).handleRequestTimeout` is **DORMANT**. A bare `grep -rn handleRequestTimeout` returns both and the live one reads as confirmation that the file you are in is live. **The dormant half also carries its own copy of the 029 defect** — `retryTimedOutRequest` resets the retry window to a hard **30 seconds** (helpers.go ~:240) and re-arms with `MonitorRequest(..., 30*time.Second)` (~:309) — so if you "fix the timeout logic" there, you have changed nothing and will believe you have.
- **the check, and it is a caller graph, not a grep for the symbol:** the cluster is unreachable because **nothing constructs it**. Walk it upward, not downward:
  ```bash
  grep -rn "NewOrchestratorHelper\|NewTimeoutMonitor" --include="*.go" .   # constructors
  grep -rn "TimeoutMonitor\|OrchestratorHelper" --include="*.go" . | grep -v "/helpers.go"   # MUST be empty
  ```
  As of 2026-08-18 the second returns **nothing**: every reference to either type lives inside `helpers.go`. `NewTimeoutMonitor` has one caller (`NewOrchestratorHelper`, :587); **`NewOrchestratorHelper` has ZERO**. `MonitorRequest`'s only call site (:309) is *inside* `retryTimedOutRequest` — a self-loop. ⚠ **Scope the claim to this module**: both constructors are **exported**, so the absence is "no caller in this repository", not "uncallable". Re-run the second grep rather than trusting this entry — an entry asserting an absence expires the moment someone adds a caller.
- **the tell that it is dormant, if you want one without the grep:** a live cluster leaves rows. `retryTimedOutRequest` would produce awaited windows of exactly **00:00:30**; the live population shows **02:00 / 03:00 / 05:00 / 15:00 / 20:00** and no 30-second windows at all.
  ```sql
  SELECT (timeout_at-sent_at)::interval(0) AS window, count(*) FROM awaited_requests
   WHERE sent_at > now()-interval '4 days' GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 DESC;
  ```
- **the remedy:** when you change the retry window, change `coordinator.go` — `retryWindow` (RSH-010) is the live one. Leave the twin, or delete the dead cluster deliberately in its own commit; do **not** "keep them in sync", because two implementations of one judgement is the drift class the council reviews for. This was raised as a HIGH objection by the `prior_art_librarian` seat on corr `7c92389a-617f-4abc-b03b-0ef84ca2239f` — the author had asserted the absence without the caller graph, and the seat was right to refuse it on that ground even though the answer came back clean.
- **relations:** RSH-010 (the live fix, and its `verify-later`) · `bugs_open/029` · `bugs_open/259` (the estate deleted a *different* nil-handle duplicate in the chassis once already — same shape, and its note says "do not go looking for the other one", which is worth reading beside this) · MEMORY [[a-helper-with-no-callers-is-not-a-refactor]]
- **source:** 2026-08-18, `bugfix_029_retry_kills_live_child` lane. Caller graph and the council exchange in `NOTES_retry_kills_live_child.md`.
- **added:** 2026-08-18, bugs_open/029 lane

### `platform/orchestration/monitoring.go` queries `orchestrator_state` — a table that DOES NOT EXIST — so "the metric counts X" is true of the source and false of every live reading

> **CORRECTED + SUPERSEDED 2026-08-18, same day, by the author of this entry.** Two things.
>
> **(1) The entry overstated reachability, and in exactly the way it warns against.** It said
> `WorkflowMonitor` "IS wired … so this is not dead-by-disuse — the endpoints are live and
> return **500** to anyone who asks". **False.** `AddMonitoringEndpoints`
> (`platform/health/monitoring.go:16`) had **ZERO callers**, so `/monitor/stuck` and
> `/monitor/metrics` were never registered on any server: nobody could reach them and no 500
> was ever produced. I read the function — it does mount handlers — and did not walk the
> caller graph, which is the same mistake this entry exists to catch. **Third instance in one
> session** (the others: `bugs_open/294`'s root-cause item 4, and describing `TimeoutMonitor`
> as blind-to-empty-`awaited_requests` when nothing constructs it). The durable lesson is the
> sibling entry's: `grep` the symbol **upward to its constructors and callers**, never just
> read the body.
>
> **(2) The code is GONE — deleted 2026-08-18 (`0e169319b`), owner-directed.**
> `platform/orchestration/monitoring.go`, `platform/health/monitoring.go`,
> `cmd/workflow-monitor/` and its orphan CronJob manifest were removed after enumerating that
> nothing reached any of them. **So the trap no longer fires on a live file** — this entry is
> kept only so the *reasoning* survives, and because the misreading it caused is still sitting
> in `bugs_open/294`'s original text. If you are here from a stale citation: the live
> active-workflow count is `internal/core-manager/admin/dashboard_handlers.go:351-354`, which
> reads the real table. Council `Council-Submitted: 25fa8173-91d5-4b1a-ad05-d35b0f7af96a`.

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/monitoring.go` (`WorkflowMonitor`, `GetStuckWorkflows`, `GetWorkflowMetrics`), `platform/health/monitoring.go` (`/monitor/stuck`, `/monitor/metrics`), `cmd/workflow-monitor`, the identifier `orchestrator_state` (SINGULAR, no trailing `s`), any claim about the fleet's active-orchestration count
- **fires when:** you reason about what the platform *observes* — "why did nothing notice this?", "the active-orchestration metric was overstated", "the instrument should have surfaced it". `monitoring.go` is the obvious place to look, it is named for the job, and its SQL is perfectly readable. Reading it tells you `RUNNING` counts as active (`WHERE status IN ('RUNNING', 'AWAITING_RESPONSES')`, :111 and :167) — and that sentence is true about the file and false about the system.
- **the mechanism:** those queries select `FROM orchestrator_state`. The real table is **`orchestration_states`** — different word, different number. `orchestrator_state` exists in no schema on the search path, so the queries do not miscount, they **error**:
  ```sql
  SELECT to_regclass('orchestrator_state'), to_regclass('public.orchestrator_state'), to_regclass('orchestration_states');
  --  (null) | (null) | orchestration_states
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orchestrator_state WHERE status IN ('RUNNING','AWAITING_RESPONSES');
  --  ERROR:  relation "orchestrator_state" does not exist
  ```
  `WorkflowMonitor` IS wired (`platform/health/monitoring.go:16` mounts the endpoints; `cmd/workflow-monitor/main.go:45` builds one), so this is not dead-by-disuse — the endpoints are live and return **500** to anyone who asks, logging `Failed to get stuck workflows` / `Failed to get workflow metrics`. Note `monitoring.go:51` reads the CORRECT table, so the file is half-right, which is exactly what makes a skim reassuring.
- **the tell, and it is an ABSENCE, so you will not get one:** nobody polls these endpoints, so the 500s sit in the logs unread. There is no wrong number to notice — the trap is that you conclude a metric was *misreporting* when it was never reporting.
- **the check, before you attribute anything to a metric:** ask the database whether the relation the code names actually exists — `SELECT to_regclass('<the exact identifier in the SQL>')` — and only then argue about the predicate. **Run it on the identifier you copied out of the Go, not the one you remember**, because `orchestration_states` and `orchestrator_state` read identically at a glance. If you want the live active-workflow count, the query that really runs is **`internal/core-manager/admin/dashboard_handlers.go:351-354`**, which reads `orchestration_states` and does count `RUNNING` as active.
- **how it bit:** `bugs_open/294` root-cause item 4 stated that `monitoring.go:111,167` counted 49 permanent corpses as healthy work and called it *"the instrument that should have surfaced this"*. It could not have. The claim was cited from the source, was internally consistent, and named the right line numbers — and the table was never there. Corrected 2026-08-18 in `bugs_closed/294` and in `016b` §10.
- **relations:** `bugs_closed/294` · `bugs_open/240` (topic pressure — `cleanup_stale_topics.go:207-215` reads the REAL table and does protect `RUNNING`) · the sibling entry below (a status nobody enumerated) · MEMORY [[a-helper-with-no-callers-is-not-a-refactor]] and [[a-doc-comment-is-not-an-enforcement-mechanism]] — same family: the code says it, nothing does it
- **source:** 2026-08-18, `bugs_open 294` lane, while verifying 294's root-cause list before fixing it
- **added:** 2026-08-18, bugs_open/294 lane

### The stale-orchestration reaper enumerates STATUSES, so any status nobody listed is immortal — and `INITIALIZED` still is (36 days, live today)

- **footprint:** `scheduled_tasks.pre_query` WHERE `name='stale-orchestration-reaper'`, `orchestration_states.status`, the CTE names `failed_dispatch` / `failed_orchs` / `failed_wedged` / `failed_running`, `platform/orchestration/actions/cleanup_stale_topics.go` (`getActiveOrchestrationTopics`), any "the reaper will clean that up" assumption
- **fires when:** you assume a non-terminal orchestration row is eventually swept, or you add a new status, or you read the reaper and see three or four healthy-looking arms and stop reading. The reaper's structure invites it: each arm is `status = '<literal>' AND last_activity < NOW() - INTERVAL '<n>'`, so its coverage is **an enumeration, not an invariant** — it reaps the statuses someone thought of, and is silent about the rest by construction.
- **the trap:** a status with no arm is not swept *slowly*, it is **never swept**. `RUNNING` was the worked case (`bugs_closed/294`: 49 rows, oldest idle 19 days through multiple fleet rolls, each pinning two Kafka topics because `getActiveOrchestrationTopics` protects `RUNNING`). A `RUNNING` arm was added 2026-08-18 (migration `463`) — **but the class is not closed, only that instance.** Measured the same day, with `RUNNING` at 0:
  ```
  status       | owner_agent_type | current_step | idle_days
  INITIALIZED  | generic          | check_health |      36.1
  ```
  `INITIALIZED` has no arm either. It is **less harmful than `RUNNING` was** — it is absent from `getActiveOrchestrationTopics`'s protected set, so it pins no topics — but it is the same defect, still open, and it is what `294`'s fix candidate 2 (reap on the INVARIANT: any non-terminal row with empty `awaited_requests` and stale `last_activity`) exists to close.
- **the check, and do it BEFORE concluding anything will be cleaned up:** read the arms out of the LIVE row, never from a migration file's intent (several migrations have rewritten this text) —
  ```sql
  SELECT pre_query FROM scheduled_tasks WHERE name='stale-orchestration-reaper';
  ```
  then census what is actually non-terminal and compare the two sets yourself:
  ```sql
  SELECT status, count(*), round(extract(epoch from (now()-min(last_activity)))/86400,1) AS oldest_days
    FROM orchestration_states WHERE status NOT IN ('COMPLETED','FAILED','CANCELLED') GROUP BY 1;
  ```
  **A status present in the census and absent from the `pre_query` is an immortality bug, today.** ⚠ Do NOT license a new arm's threshold with an age census alone: after a sweep it reads 0 in every band and so cannot come out otherwise — `294` was licensed instead by proving in the code that `RUNNING` has one writer (`state.go:1428`), one caller (`coordinator.go:765`), and a next-write that flips it straight back (`coordinator.go:868`).
- **and do not expect the other recovery paths to catch it:** `TimeoutMonitor` is **DORMANT** — nothing constructs it (see the `handleRequestTimeout` entry above) — and `handleOrchestrationStatus` (`coordinator.go:740-796`) has cases for `INITIALIZED`/`EXECUTING_STEP`/`AWAITING_RESPONSES`/`COMPLETED`/`FAILED` and a `default:` that returns `unknown orchestration status: %s`. So for an unenumerated status the message-driven path **rejects** the row rather than recovering it. The reaper is the only sweeper there is, which is also why a reaper arm is the RIGHT fix and not a cheap one: a pod that dies mid-transition cannot recover itself.
- **relations:** `bugs_closed/294` (the `RUNNING` case, with the induced both-directions test) · `bugs_open/240` (topic pressure this feeds) · `bugs_closed/289` (the producer that filled the hole) · the `handleRequestTimeout` entry (why `TimeoutMonitor` is not a backstop) · the sibling entry above (why the metric did not surface it) · migration `463_reaper_running_arm.sql` + its `_ROLLBACK` sidecar
- **source:** 2026-08-18, `bugs_open 294` lane; census and induced test in `bugs_closed/294`'s Closure section
- **added:** 2026-08-18, bugs_open/294 lane

### The tool-birth guard counts tag SUBSTRINGS, so a generated tool that merely MENTIONS a structural tag is refused at birth — with an error blaming truncation that its own recorded evidence disproves

- **footprint:** `platform/orchestration/actions/plan_sections_action.go:1853` (`toolTemplateValid`) · `platform/orchestration/actions/component_write_guard.go:146` (`balancedPairs`) · `create_tool_component_action.go:127-146` (the birth refusal) · any `add_tool` work item whose tool handles HTML/XML/markup · `agent_error_log.error_code='tool_birth_truncation_blocked'`
- **fires when:** you file a perfectly good `add_tool` for a minifier, formatter, escaper, sanitiser, template previewer or code-snippet tool. The generation succeeds and is complete; the write is refused. The error reads *"refusing to persist truncated tool … the generation was cut; regenerate"*, so you go looking for a token-limit truncation, find `output_tokens` far below `max_tokens`, and have nothing to go on. Re-running sometimes "fixes" it, which is the worst outcome — it teaches you the generation is flaky when the predicate is deterministic on the text it happened to produce.
- **the mechanism:** the gate is `strings.Count(folded, "<script") > strings.Count(folded, "</script>")`, and the same for `<style`, `<section`, `<div`, `<fieldset` — a **plain substring count over the whole file**, case-folded, with no parsing and no awareness of JavaScript strings, regular expressions, code comments or visible prose. A tool that manipulates markup mentions those tags in its own source by necessity. One unpaired mention — a comment, a regex `/<style[^>]*>/`, or body copy explaining the tool — tips opens over closes. Calibrated 0-false-positive on 2026-07-20 against 27 tools, **none of which manipulated HTML**; the first that did were created 2026-08-17.
- **the tell:** `agent_error_log` context for `tool_birth_truncation_blocked` carries **`"ends_cleanly": true`** — the guard's *other* half passed, so the document terminates properly and the rejection is purely tag-balance. Pair it with `SELECT max_tokens, output_tokens FROM llm_call_log WHERE agent_type='tool-generator' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 1;` — **13,979 of 32,000 measured 2026-08-18.** Both signals say "not truncated" while the message says it was.
